6.16. Then, through parley with the captives, their wildness gradually softened, they surrendered to the king. Nor was harsher measure taken against those who gave themselves up.
6.17. After laying waste the fields of Persia and reducing several villages to his power, he came among the Mardi, a warlike nation and far removed from the rest of the Persians in their way of life. They dig caves in the mountains, in which they hide themselves and their wives and children; they feed on the flesh of cattle or wild beasts.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
6.18. Their women too have no temper softer than their nature would suggest: their hair sticks out, shaggy; their dress reaches above the knee; they bind their foreheads with a sling: this serves both as a headdress and as a weapon.
6.19. But this nation too the same rush of fortune subdued. And so, on the thirtieth day after he had set out from Persepolis, he returned to the same place.
6.20. Then he gave gifts to his friends and to the rest according to each man's desert. Almost everything that he had taken in that city was distributed.
7.1. But those vast goods of his mind, that natural genius by which he surpassed all kings, that steadfastness in facing dangers, that swiftness in undertaking and accomplishing his designs, that good faith toward those who surrendered, that clemency toward captives, that temperance even in pleasures permitted and customary—all this he defiled with a craving for wine that was past bearing.
7.2. While his enemy and rival for the throne was at that very moment renewing the war, while those he had lately subdued were spurning his new dominion, he was holding banquets by day, at which women were present—not such as it would be wrong to violate, for they were concubines accustomed to live with the soldiery more freely than was seemly.
7.3. One of these, Thais, herself drunk, declared that he would win the greatest favor among all the Greeks if he ordered the palace of the Persians to be set ablaze: this was what those whose cities the barbarians had destroyed were looking for.
7.4. As a drunken harlot was delivering judgment on so great a matter, one or two, themselves loaded with wine, assented.
7.5. The king too, more greedy for wine than able to bear it, said: "Why then do we not avenge Greece and put torches to the city?" All had grown hot with wine; and so they rose, drunk, to set fire to the city that they had spared when armed. The king first cast fire into the palace, then the guests and the attendants and the concubines.
7.6. The palace had been built largely of cedar, which, quickly catching the fire, spread the conflagration far and wide. When the army, encamped not far from the city, saw it, supposing the fire accidental, it ran together to bring help.
7.7. But when they came to the vestibule of the palace, they saw the king himself still heaping up torches. So, abandoning the water they had brought, they themselves began to throw dry timber onto the blaze.
7.8. Such was the end of the palace of all the East, whence so many nations had once sought their laws, the homeland of so many kings, the one-time terror of Greece, which had launched a fleet of a thousand ships and armies that flooded over Europe, bridging the sea with moles and cutting through mountains into whose caverns the strait was let in.
7.9. Nor even in the long age that followed its destruction did it rise again. The Macedonian kings laid waste other cities, which the Parthians now hold: of this one not a trace would be found, were not the river Araxes there to point it out. It had flowed not far from the walls: the neighboring people believe, rather than know, that from it the city stood twenty stades distant.
7.10. The Macedonians were ashamed that so famous a city had been destroyed by a king at his revels; so the matter was turned into earnest, and they constrained themselves to believe that this was indeed the way it ought to have been destroyed.
7.11. As for the king himself, it is agreed that as soon as rest restored his mind, weighed down by drunkenness, he repented and said that the Persians would have paid a heavier penalty to the Greeks, had they been compelled to behold him upon the throne and in the palace of Xerxes.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
7.12. On the next day he gave thirty talents as a gift to the Lycian, the guide of the road by which he had entered Persia. From here he crossed into the region of Media, where a reinforcement of new soldiers from Cilicia met him. There were five thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry; over both Plato the Athenian was in command. Strengthened by these forces, he resolved to pursue Darius.
8.1. Darius had by now reached Ecbatana. This city is the capital of Media: the Parthians now hold it, and it is their summer seat. He had resolved next to make for Bactra, but, fearing that he might be overtaken by Alexander's swiftness, he changed his plan and his route.
8.2. Alexander was fifteen hundred stades distant from him, but no interval now seemed long enough against his speed; and so Darius was preparing himself for battle rather than for flight.
8.3. Thirty thousand infantry followed him, among whom were four thousand Greeks, unconquered to the very end in their long-standing loyalty toward the king.
8.4. A band of slingers and archers too had filled out four thousand; besides these there were three thousand three hundred cavalry, mostly of the Bactrians.
8.5. Bessus was in command, the governor of the Bactrian region. With this column Darius turned a little aside from the military road, having ordered the camp-followers and the guards of the baggage to go on ahead.
8.6. Then, summoning a council, he said: "If fortune had joined me with cowards, men who value any kind of life more than an honorable death, I should be silent rather than waste words in vain.
8.7. But having found proof, greater than I could wish, both of your valor and of your loyalty, I ought to strive all the more to be worthy of such friends than to doubt whether you are still like yourselves.
8.8. Out of so many thousands who have been under my command, twice when I was conquered, twice when I fled, you have followed me.
8.9. Your loyalty and steadfastness make me believe that I am a king. Traitors and deserters reign in my cities—not, by Heaven, because they are judged worthy of such honor, but that your minds may be tempted by their rewards. Yet you have chosen to follow my fortune rather than the victor's, most worthy men, to whom, if I cannot, may the gods render thanks on my behalf.
8.10. And, by Heaven, they will render them. No posterity will be so deaf, no report so ungrateful, as not to bear you to the skies with the praises you are owed. So even if I had entertained a plan of flight, from which my spirit utterly shrinks, yet, relying on your valor, I would have gone to meet the enemy.
8.11. For how long shall I be an exile within my own kingdom, and flee through the borders of my own empire before a foreign and newcome king, when I may make trial of the fortune of war and either recover what I have lost or end my days by an honorable death?
8.12. Unless perhaps it is better to await the victor's pleasure, and after the example of Mazaeus and Mithrenes to receive on sufferance the kingship of a single nation, so that he may now prefer to indulge his glory rather than his anger.
8.13. May the gods not permit anyone either to take this crown from my head or to bestow it on me; nor will I lose my empire while I live, and the same shall be the end of my reign as of my breath.
8.14. If this is your spirit, if this your resolve, then freedom is won for every one of you. None of you shall be forced to bear the disdain of the Macedonians, none their haughty look: each man's own right hand shall bring him either vengeance for so many ills or an end of them.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
8.15. For my part, how changeable fortune is, I myself am the proof, and not without reason do I look for her milder turns. But if the gods turn away from wars however just and righteous, brave men will yet be permitted to die honorably.
8.16. By the glories of your ancestors, who held the realms of all the East with memorable renown; by those men to whom Macedonia once paid tribute; by so many fleets of ships sent against Greece; by so many trophies of kings—I beg and implore you to take up a spirit worthy of your nobility and your nation,
8.17. and to face, with the same steadfastness of soul with which you have endured the past, whatever chance shall bring hereafter: as for me, surely either a glorious victory or my downfall will ennoble me forever."
9.1. As Darius spoke thus, the appearance of present peril had struck the hearts and spirits of all alike with horror, and neither counsel nor voice was at hand, when Artabazus, the oldest of his friends—whom we have said above was once the guest-friend of Philip—said: "We, for our part, clothed in our most precious raiment and adorned with the greatest splendor we can muster, will follow the king into the battle line, in this mind: that we hope for victory but do not refuse death."
9.2. The rest received this speech with approval; but Nabarzanes, who was in the same council, had, with Bessus, entered into a partnership in a crime unheard of before: they had resolved to seize their king through the soldiers whom both commanded and to bind him, in this mind: that, if Alexander pursued them, by handing the king over alive they might win the victor's favor, reckoning that they would surely have made a great prize in capturing Darius; but if they could escape him, then, having killed Darius, they would seize the kingdom for themselves and renew the war.
9.3. When they had long turned this parricide over in their minds, Nabarzanes, preparing an approach for his wicked hope, said: "I know that I am about to give an opinion which at first sight will be by no means pleasing to your ears; but physicians too cure graver diseases with harsh remedies, and the helmsman, when he fears shipwreck, ransoms whatever can be saved by jettisoning the rest.
9.4. Yet I do not advise that you suffer any loss, but that you preserve yourself and your kingdom by a sound policy. We are entering the war with the gods against us, and a stubborn fortune does not cease to press the Persians: there is need of fresh beginnings and fresh auspices. Hand over the auspices and the command meanwhile to another, who shall be called king only until the enemy withdraws from Asia, and then, as victor, shall restore the kingdom to you.
9.5. And reason promises that this will soon come to pass: Bactra is untouched, the Indians and the Sacae are in your power, so many peoples, so many armies, so many thousands of horse and foot have their strength ready for renewing the struggle, so that a greater mass of war remains than has been spent.
9.6. Why do we rush like wild beasts to a destruction not forced upon us? It is the mark of brave men rather to despise death than to hate life:
9.7. often it is the weariness of toil that drives cowards to set themselves at naught. But valor leaves nothing untried. In any case death is the last resort of all, and it is enough not to go to it slothfully.
9.8. Therefore, if we make for Bactra, which is the safest refuge, let us appoint the governor of that region, Bessus, as king for the time being: when matters are settled, he will restore the empire to you, its rightful king, in good faith."

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
9.9. It is no wonder that Darius did not master his feelings, although how great a crime lay beneath that impious speech was hidden from him. And so he said: "Vilest of slaves, have you found the longed-for moment in which to lay bare your treason?"
9.10. And, drawing his scimitar, he seemed about to kill him, had not Bessus and the Bactrians quickly stood around—as though pleading for the man, with a sorrowful air, but in truth ready, if Darius persisted, to bind him.
9.11. Nabarzanes meanwhile slipped away, and soon Bessus too followed: they ordered the forces they commanded to withdraw from the rest of the army, intending to hold a secret council.
9.12. Artabazus, beginning with an opinion suited to the present fortune, set about soothing Darius, reminding him again and again of the times: let him bear with an even mind the folly or the error of his own men, such as they were. Alexander, he said, was already pressing upon him, formidable even if all stood by; what would happen if those who had pursued his flight were estranged?
9.13. Reluctantly Darius yielded to Artabazus, and although he had resolved to break camp, yet, since the minds of all were in turmoil, he halted in the same place. But, stunned with grief and despair alike, he shut himself up in his tent.
9.14. So in the camp, which was ruled by no man's command, there were various movements of feeling, nor was there deliberation in common as before.
9.15. Patron, the commander of the Greek soldiers, ordered his men to take up arms and be ready to carry out his command.
9.16. The Persians had withdrawn apart: Bessus was with the Bactrians and was trying to draw off the Persians, holding out the riches of Bactra and of the untouched region, and at the same time the dangers that threatened those who stayed. The voice of all the Persians was much the same: that it was wickedness to desert the king.
9.17. Amid this Artabazus discharged all the duties of a commander: he went round the tents of the Persians, exhorting, advising, now individuals, now all together, nor did he leave off until it was clear enough that they would do his bidding. The same man with difficulty prevailed on Darius to take food and to turn his mind to affairs.
10.1. But Bessus and Nabarzanes resolved to carry out the crime they had long meditated, inflamed with desire for the kingdom: for while Darius was safe, they could not hope for such great resources.
10.2. For among those nations the majesty of kings is preeminent: at the very name the barbarians gather, and the reverence for their former fortune follows it into adversity.
10.3. The region they governed inflamed their impious spirits, second to none of those nations in arms, in men, and in extent of territory: it holds a third part of Asia, and its multitude of young men equaled the armies Darius had lost.
10.4. And so they scorned not only him but Alexander too, meaning to draw from there the resources of empire, if it should fall to them to gain possession of the king.
10.5. After long pondering everything, they decided to seize the king through the Bactrian soldiers, who were ready for any obedience, and to send a messenger to Alexander to inform him that Darius was being kept alive:
10.6. but if—what they feared—he should spurn the betrayal, they would kill Darius and make for Bactra with a force of their own nations.
10.7. But Darius could not be seized openly, since so many thousands of Persians would bring aid to their king; the loyalty of the Greeks too was feared.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
10.8. So they tried to gain by treachery what they could not by force: they resolved to feign repentance for their withdrawal and to excuse their alarm before the king.
10.9. Meanwhile men were sent to work upon the Persians. Now with hope, now with fear they swayed the soldiers' minds: that those men were thrusting their heads beneath the ruin of the state, were being dragged to destruction, when Bactra lay open to receive them with goods and an opulence greater than they could conceive in their minds.
10.10. While they were busy with these schemes, Artabazus came upon them—whether by the king's command or of his own accord—declaring that Darius had been appeased and that the same degree of friendship lay open to them with the king.
10.11. They, with tears, now sought to clear themselves, now begged Artabazus to defend their cause and carry their prayers.
10.12. Thus, the night being passed, at the rising of the light Bessus and Nabarzanes with the Bactrian soldiers were present in the vestibule of the headquarters, putting forward the show of customary duty as a screen for their hidden crime. Darius, when the signal to set out was given, mounted his chariot after his old custom.
10.13. Nabarzanes and the other parricides, prostrating themselves on the ground, did reverence to him whom a little later they would hold in chains; they even shed tears as tokens of repentance: so ready a thing is dissimulation to the human spirit.
10.14. Their prayers, then, suppliantly offered, drove Darius—simple and gentle by nature—not only to believe what they affirmed, but even to weep.
10.15. And not even then did they repent of the crime they had plotted, when they looked upon what kind of king and what kind of man they were deceiving. He indeed, careless of the peril that hung over him, was hastening to escape the hands of Alexander, which alone he feared.
11.1. But Patron, the commander of the Greeks, charged his men to put on the arms which before they had carried in their packs, and to be ready and intent on his every command.
11.2. He himself followed the king's chariot, watching for an occasion to address him; for he had foreseen the crime of Bessus. But Bessus, fearing this very thing, would not leave the chariot—a guard, more truly, than a companion.
11.3. So Patron long hesitated, and, often called back by conversation, wavering between loyalty and fear, kept his eyes on the king.
11.4. When at last the king turned his eyes that way, he ordered Bubaces, a eunuch among those nearest, who was following the chariot, to ask whether Patron wished to say anything to him. Patron answered that he did indeed, but that he wished to speak with him with the witnesses removed; and, ordered to come nearer without an interpreter—
11.5. for Darius was not unacquainted with the Greek tongue—he said: "O king, of fifty thousand Greeks we few survive, companions of your every fortune, and in this your present state the same as we were when you flourished; ready to make for whatever lands you choose, in place of homeland and home.
11.6. Your prosperous and your adverse fortunes have bound us to you. By this loyalty unconquered I beg and implore you: set up your tent in our camp; suffer us to be the guards of your person. We have given up Greece; there is no Bactra for us; all our hope is in you—would that it were so for the rest as well. There is no need to say more. I, a foreigner and an alien, would not demand the guardianship of your person, if I believed another could provide it."

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
11.7. Bessus, although he was ignorant of the Greek tongue, yet, his conscience pricking him, believed that Patron had surely laid information; and when the speech of the Greeks was interpreted, secretly, all doubt was removed. But Darius—as far as could be gathered from his look—by no means terrified, began to ask Patron the reason for the advice he brought.
11.8. Patron, thinking it should be put off no longer, said: "Bessus and Nabarzanes are plotting against you; you are in the last extremity of your fortune and your life,
11.9. and this day shall be the last either for the parricides or for you." And Patron indeed had won the splendid glory of having tried to save the king.
11.10. Let those mock at loyalty, if they will, to whom perchance it is settled that human affairs are rolled and driven at random, and that no chain of hidden and long-foreordained causes carries each man through his own ordered course by an unchangeable law:
11.11. Darius at any rate answered that, although the loyalty of the Greek soldiers was known to him, he would nevertheless never withdraw from his own countrymen. It was harder for him to condemn than to be deceived. Whatever chance should bring, he preferred to suffer it among his own rather than become a deserter. He perished too late, if his own soldiers did not wish him safe.
11.12. Patron, despairing of the king's safety, returned to those he commanded, prepared to make every trial for loyalty's sake.
12.1. But Bessus had conceived an impulse to kill the king at once; yet, fearing that he could not win Alexander's favor unless he handed him over alive, he put off the design of his crime to the next night, and began to give thanks to Darius for having prudently and warily avoided the treachery of a treacherous man who was already looking to Alexander's power: he would have carried the king's head as a gift to the enemy.
12.2. Nor was it any wonder, he said, that a man hired for pay had everything for sale; without pledge, without home, an exile from the whole world, a doubtful enemy, he was carried this way and that at the nod of those who hired him.
12.3. Then, as Bessus cleared himself and called the gods of his fathers to witness his good faith, Darius assented with his countenance, in no doubt that the Greeks were reporting the truth; but matters had come to such a pass that it was as dangerous not to trust his own men as to be deceived.
12.4. There were thirty thousand, whose fickleness, leaning toward crime, was feared; Patron had four thousand: if Darius had entrusted his safety to these, condemning the loyalty of his own countrymen, he saw that he would be offering an excuse for the parricide. And so he preferred to be done to death undeservingly rather than with cause.
12.5. To Bessus, nevertheless, as he cleared himself of the charge of treachery, he answered that he had seen no less of Alexander's justice than of his valor. Those were deceived who looked for a reward of betrayal from him: of violated loyalty no one would be a sharper avenger and punisher.
12.6. And now night was coming on, when the Persians, after their usual fashion, laid aside their arms and scattered to fetch necessaries from the nearest village. But the Bactrians, as Bessus had ordered, stood under arms.
12.7. Meanwhile Darius ordered Artabazus to be summoned, and, when he had set forth what Patron had reported, Artabazus did not doubt that he must cross over into the camp of the Greeks: the Persians too, once the peril was made known, would follow.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
12.8. Resigned to his lot and now incapable of any wholesome counsel, he embraced Artabazus—his one help in that fortune—as though to look upon him for the last time; and, both bathed in mutual tears, he ordered him to be torn from his clinging embrace; then, his head veiled, that he might not gaze upon him departing amid groans as from a funeral pyre, he flung his body face down upon the ground.
12.9. Then indeed those accustomed to his guard, who ought to have protected the king's safety even at the peril of their lives, slipped away, secretly from the armed men whom they now believed to be approaching, not reckoning that they would be a match for them. So there was a vast solitude in the tent, a few eunuchs standing about the king, because they had nowhere to go.
12.10. But he, the witnesses removed, long turned over in his mind one plan after another. And now, loathing the solitude which a little before he had sought as a solace, he ordered Bubaces to be called.
12.11. Looking at him, he said: "Go, take thought for yourselves, having shown to the last—as was fitting—the loyalty owed to your king: I await here the law of my fate. Perhaps you wonder that I do not make an end of my life: I would rather die by another's crime than by my own."
12.12. At these words the eunuch filled with his lamentation not the tent only but the camp as well. Then others burst in and, their garments rent, with mournful, barbaric wailing began to bewail the king.
12.13. The Persians, when the cry was carried to them, struck with fear, dared neither to take up arms—lest they fall upon the Bactrians—nor to remain quiet, lest they seem impiously to desert the king.
12.14. A varied and discordant cry, without leader and without command, echoed through the whole camp. To Bessus and Nabarzanes their men reported that the king had killed himself—the wailing had deceived them—;
12.15. and so they galloped up at full speed, followed by those they had chosen for the service of the crime; and, when they had entered the tent, since the eunuchs declared that the king was alive, they ordered him to be seized and bound.
12.16. The king, a little before borne in his chariot and honored with the auspices of the gods and the highest honors, now with no help from abroad, a captive of his own slaves, was set in a foul cart covered all over with hides.
12.17. The king's money and furnishings were plundered as though by the law of war, and, laden with the spoil won by their last crime, they pressed on in flight.
12.18. Artabazus, with those who obeyed his command and with the Greek soldiers, made for Parthiene, reckoning everything safer than the company of the parricides.
12.19. The Persians, weighed down above all by the promises of Bessus, since there was no one else to follow, joined themselves to the Bactrians, overtaking their column on the third day.
12.20. Yet, that the king might not go unhonored, they bound Darius with fetters of gold, fortune ever devising fresh mockeries. And lest perchance he could be recognized by his royal garb, they had covered the cart with mean hides; unknown men drove the beasts, so that he could not be pointed out to those who asked along the way; the guards followed at a distance.
13.1. Alexander, on hearing that Darius had moved from Ecbatana, abandoned the route he was making for, into Media, and pressed on briskly to pursue the fugitive.
13.2. He reached Tabae—a town in the farthest part of Paraetacene—; there deserters reported that Darius was making for Bactra in headlong flight.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
13.3. Then he learned more certain news from Bagistanes the Babylonian, who affirmed that the king was not yet in chains, but in peril either of death or of bonds.
13.4. The king, summoning his leaders, said: "The greatest task remains, but the shortest toil. Darius, deserted by his own men or overpowered, is not far off: in that one body lies our victory, and so great a prize is the reward of speed."
13.5. All cried out together that they were ready to follow him: let him spare neither toil nor danger. So he led his column swiftly, more in the manner of a race than a march, not even relaxing the day's toil with the rest of night.
13.6. And so he advanced five hundred stades, and came to the village in which Bessus had seized Darius.
13.7. There Melon, the interpreter of Darius, was taken: sick in body, he had not been able to keep up with the column, and, caught by the king's swiftness, he pretended to be a deserter. From him Alexander learned what had been done.
13.8. But the weary men needed rest: so to six thousand chosen cavalry he added three hundred whom they called dimachae. These carried heavier arms on their backs but rode on horseback; when occasion and place required, they were a line of infantry.
13.9. While Alexander was about these matters, Orsines and Mithracenes came to him: hating the parricide of Bessus, they had deserted and reported that the Persians were five hundred stades off, and that they themselves would point out a shorter road.
13.10. The arrival of the deserters was welcome to the king. So at first nightfall, with the same men as guides, he entered the road pointed out to him with a light force of cavalry, the phalanx being ordered to follow as fast as it could hasten. He himself, advancing in a hollow square, so governed the march that the foremost could be joined with the hindmost.
13.11. They had advanced three hundred stades, when Brochubelus met them, the son of Mazaeus, once governor of Syria: he too, a deserter, reported that Bessus was no more than two hundred stades distant, and that the army, being greedy for plunder, was advancing in disorder and without array.
13.12. They seemed to be making for Hyrcania: if he hurried to pursue them as they straggled, he would overtake them. Darius was still alive. To a man otherwise eager, the deserter had added the desire of overtaking them: so, putting in the spurs, they went at full gallop. And now the din of the enemy entering on their march could be heard, but a cloud of dust had cut off the view. So he checked his course a little while, until the dust settled.
13.13. And now they had been sighted by the barbarians, and had themselves caught sight of the departing column—by no means a match for it, had Bessus had as much spirit for battle as he had had for parricide. For the barbarians were superior both in numbers and in strength; and, fresh, they were about to engage with men worn out.
13.14. But the name of Alexander and his fame—the greatest factor of all in war—turned them, panic-stricken, to flight.
13.15. Bessus, however, and the rest who shared in his crime, having reached the cart of Darius, began to urge him to mount a horse and snatch himself from the enemy by flight.
13.16. He called the avenging gods to witness, and imploring the good faith of Alexander, refused to accompany the parricides. Then indeed, kindled with anger too, they hurled weapons at the king and, having pierced him with many wounds, left him.
13.17. They wounded the beasts too, that they might not be able to draw him farther, and killed the two servants who attended the king.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
13.18. This deed accomplished, that they might scatter the traces of their flight, Nabarzanes made for Hyrcania, Bessus for Bactra, each with a few horsemen attending. The barbarians, abandoned by their leaders, scattered as hope or fear led each; only five hundred cavalry had gathered together, still uncertain whether it were better to resist or to flee.
13.19. Alexander, on learning of the enemy's panic, sent Nicanor with part of the cavalry to check their flight, and himself followed with the rest. About three thousand of those who resisted were killed; the remaining column, like a herd of cattle, was driven along untouched, the king ordering that there be no slaughter.
13.20. There was none of the captives who could point out the cart of Darius: they searched each one as they laid hold of it, yet no trace of the king's flight appeared.
13.21. Scarcely three thousand cavalry followed Alexander in his haste. But upon those who followed more slowly the whole columns of the fleeing fell.
13.22. Scarcely credible to tell, the captives were more than those who took them: so utterly had fortune driven all sense out of the terrified men, that they could not clearly perceive either the fewness of the enemy or their own numbers.
13.23. Meanwhile the beasts that were carrying Darius, with none to guide them, had turned off the military road and, led astray, had come after four stades to a halt in a certain valley, worn out by the heat and by their wounds alike.
13.24. Not far off was a spring: to it, pointed out by men who knew the country, Polystratus, a Macedonian, parched with thirst, came; and, while he drank water scooped up in his helmet, he caught sight of weapons fixed in the bodies of the failing beasts.
13.25. And wondering that they had been stabbed rather than driven off, he caught the groan of a man half alive. So, after the manner of human nature, eager to see what might be concealed in that cart, he drew apart the hides with which it was covered and found Darius, pierced with many wounds. For the royal garb and the golden chains with which he had been bound by the parricides removed all doubt. Darius was not without knowledge of the Greek tongue, and he gave thanks to the gods, who after so many evils had granted him this comfort at least, that he should not pour out his last breath utterly alone in the wilderness. "And so," he said, "whoever you are among mortals, by the common lot of men—from which not even the greatest kings are exempt, as the present spectacle warns you—I ask and beseech you to carry these instructions to Alexander: that of all the things I have suffered—by far the most grievous—not even this end of an incredible calamity has fallen upon me so heavily as that, after such great services rendered to me and mine, I had to live as an enemy toward the most merciful of victors, and now must die ungrateful to him. But—if there is any power with the gods in the last prayers of the wretched, and if some divinity hears the prayers poured out with the very breath of life—may he, safe and unharmed, set far above the lot of my fortune and the envy of the gods, pass a glorious age upon the throne of Cyrus, and, mindful of his own valor, suffer my mother and my children to have a place with him such as they have earned by their loyalty and obedience. But upon the parricides may a swift destruction fall, which Alexander will inflict—if not out of pity for an unhappy enemy, then at least out of hatred for their crimes, and lest such deeds break out unpunished to the destruction of other kings and of himself as well." After this, when he was tormented by thirst, revived by water brought to him through Polystratus, he said: "And so this too has been ordained to come, as the last and crowning point of such great calamities, that I cannot render thanks to one who has deserved well of me: but Alexander will repay him, and the gods will repay Alexander." Then he stretched out his right hand, and, ordering it to be carried to Alexander as a pledge of his royal faith, having grasped the hand of Polystratus, he breathed out his soul. Whether Alexander came upon him while he was still breathing is uncertain: this much is agreed, that on learning of the pitiable end of the wealthiest of kings he shed very many tears, and at once, drawing off his own cloak, covered the body, and ordered it to be carried with great honor to his own people, that, tended after the royal custom of the Persians, it might be laid in the tombs of his ancestors. The treachery of the men by whom Darius, in return for the highest benefits, suffered a most cruel death—horrible and accursed though it was of its own nature—was branded with the more conspicuous infamy for posterity by the wondrous fidelity of a certain dog, which, abandoned by all his familiars, alone stood by him and rendered to him as he died the same fawning love it had shown him living. Such was the end of life that fell to him whom but now men thought themselves to be insulting if they did not salute him as king of kings and kinsman of the gods; and once again it was proved by a great example that no one lies more open to fortune than the man who, adorned with her many benefits, has taken her yoke upon his neck with his whole strength.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text: 1a.1. While these things were going on in Asia, affairs were not peaceful even in Greece and Macedonia. Among the Lacedaemonians there reigned Agis, the son of Archidamus, who had fallen while bringing aid to the Tarentines on the very day on which Philip conquered the Athenians at Chaeronea. This Agis, a rival of Alexander's valor, kept urging his fellow citizens not to suffer Greece to be oppressed any longer by the servitude of the Macedonians: unless they provided for it in good time, the same yoke would pass to themselves. They must therefore exert themselves while the Persians still had some strength to resist; once these were crushed, they would in vain remember their ancestral liberty against so monstrous a power. With their spirits so kindled, they watched for an occasion to set war in motion. Encouraged, then, by the prosperous outcome of Memnon's affairs, they began to share their counsels with him; and after he was cut off by an untimely death in the very beginning of his successes, they pressed on no less vigorously. But Agis, having gone to Pharnabazus and Autophradates, obtained thirty talents of silver and ten triremes, which he sent to his brother Agesilaus to sail to Crete, an island whose inhabitants were torn between the Lacedaemonians and the Macedonians by their conflicting allegiances. Envoys too were sent to Darius to ask for a larger sum of money and more ships for the war. And the disaster at Issus—for that had now intervened—so far from interrupting these plans of theirs, even furthered them. For Alexander, in pursuit of the fugitive, was being carried day by day into more distant regions, and a great multitude of mercenaries had withdrawn in flight from the battle itself into Greece: of these Agis hired eight thousand with his money, and by their service recovered most of the cities of the Cretans. Then, when Memnon, sent into Thrace by Alexander, had driven the barbarians to revolt, and Antipater had led an army out of Macedonia into Thrace to crush it, the Lacedaemonians, briskly seizing the opportunity of the moment, drew the whole Peloponnese, save a few cities, over to their side; and, having raised an army of twenty thousand infantry with two thousand cavalry, they conferred the supreme command upon Agis. Antipater, on learning this, settled the war in Thrace on whatever terms he could, and, hastily returning into Greece, gathered auxiliaries from the friendly and allied states. When these had assembled, he mustered some forty thousand soldiers. A strong force too had come from the Peloponnese; but because he had learned that their loyalty was doubtful, he concealed his suspicion and thanked them for having come to defend Alexander's dignity against the Lacedaemonians: he would write of it to the king, who would render thanks for it in due time. For the present there was no need of larger forces: so let them return home, the obligation of their alliance discharged. Then he sent messengers to Alexander to inform him of the disturbance in Greece. And these at last caught up with the king at Bactra, when in the meantime the affair had been settled by Antipater's victory and the death of Agis in Arcadia. The king, having long since learned of the rising of the Lacedaemonians, had taken what precautions he could, separated as he was by the spaces of so many lands: he had ordered Amphoterus to sail into the Peloponnese with the Cyprian and Phoenician ships, and Menetes to carry three thousand talents to the sea, so as to supply Antipater with money from close at hand, as much as he should learn he needed. For he had clearly perceived how great a weight the turn of that disturbance would have on everything; though afterward, on receiving the news of the victory, comparing that struggle with his own affairs, he jested that it had been a battle of mice. But the beginnings of that war were by no means unfavorable to the Lacedaemonians. Near Corrhagum, a fortress of Macedonia, they had engaged the soldiers of Antipater and come off victors; and the report of the deed well done brought even those who had watched fortune with wavering minds to join their alliance. Of the cities of Elis and Achaea, Pellene alone spurned the league, and in Arcadia Megalopolis, faithful to the Macedonians for the memory of Philip, by whom it had been treated with kindnesses. But Megalopolis, besieged, was not far from surrender, had not Antipater at last come to its relief. He, after he had pitched his camp opposite theirs and saw himself superior in the number of his soldiers and in his other equipment, resolved to decide the whole matter by battle as soon as possible; nor did the Lacedaemonians decline the contest. So the battle was joined, which crushed the Spartan power most grievously. For when, trusting in the narrowness of the place in which they fought, where they believed the enemy would have no use of his numbers, they had engaged most bravely, and the Macedonians resisted most stubbornly, much blood was shed. But after Antipater again and again sent fresh troops to the aid of his men as they labored, the line of the Lacedaemonians was driven in and gave ground a little. Agis, perceiving this, threw himself with the royal cohort,

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
1.1. which was made up of the bravest men, into the very crisis of the battle; and, cutting down those who resisted most readily, he drove back a great part of the enemy.
1.2. The victors had begun to flee, and, as they too eagerly pursued and were drawn down onto level ground, they fell unavenged; but as soon as there was a place where they could stand, the fight went on with equal strength.
1.3. Among all the Lacedaemonians, however, the king stood out, not only in the splendor of his arms and his person, but also in greatness of spirit, in which alone he could not be conquered.
1.4. He was assailed on every side, now hand to hand, now from a distance; and for a long time, sweeping his arms about, he caught some weapons on his shield and avoided others with his body, until, his thigh pierced through and much blood lost, they failed him as he fought.
1.5. So his armor-bearers caught him on his own shield and were hastily carrying him into the camp, though he could scarcely endure the jolting of his wounds.
1.6. Yet the Lacedaemonians did not give up the fight; and as soon as they were able to take a place fairer to themselves than to the enemy, with ranks closed up they received the line that came flooding loosely against them.
1.7. No fiercer crisis has been handed down to memory. The armies of two of the most renowned nations in war fought with the fortune of battle even between them:
1.8. the Lacedaemonians looked to their ancient glories, the Macedonians to their present ones; the one fought for liberty, the other for dominion; the Lacedaemonians lacked a leader, the Macedonians the room.
1.9. The manifold turns even of that single day now increased the hope, now the fear of each side, as though fortune were on purpose making the contest even between the bravest men.
1.10. But the narrowness of the place in which the battle was locked did not allow them to engage with their whole strength: more men, then, looked on than had entered the fight, and those who were beyond the cast of a missile kindled their comrades' courage with their shouting, each in turn.
1.11. At last the line of the Laconians began to flag, their arms slippery and scarcely held for the sweat, and then began to give ground.
1.12. When, the enemy pressing, they fled more openly, the victor pursued them as they scattered, and, having traversed at a run all the ground that the Laconian line had held, he made for Agis himself.
1.13. He, when he saw the flight of his men and the enemy close at hand, ordered himself to be set down; and, having tested his limbs to see whether they could follow the impulse of his spirit,
1.14. after he perceived that they failed, he raised himself on his knees, and, briskly taking up his helmet, protecting his body with his shield, he brandished his spear in his right hand, even challenging the enemy,
1.15. if any dared to strip the spoils from a fallen man. Nor was there anyone who could bring himself to come to close quarters: he was assailed with missiles from afar, and turning those very weapons back upon the enemy, until a lance was fixed in his bare breast. When this was torn out of the wound, he caught his drooping and failing head for a moment upon his shield; then, as his breath ebbed away together with his blood, dying he sank down upon his arms.
1.16. There fell of the Lacedaemonians five thousand three hundred, of the Macedonians not more than a thousand; but scarcely anyone returned to the camp who was not wounded. This victory crushed not only Sparta and her allies, but all who had been awaiting the fortune of the war.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
1.17. Nor did it escape Antipater that the faces of those who congratulated him were at variance with their hearts; but, since he desired to end the war, he had need to be deceived; and although the fortune of affairs pleased him, yet he feared the ill will that would arise, because the matter was greater than the measure of a deputy could contain.
1.18. For Alexander had wished his enemies to be conquered, but was vexed, though in silence, that Antipater had conquered, judging that whatever fell to another's glory was taken from his own.
1.19. So Antipater, who knew his temper well, did not dare to exercise the rights of victory himself, but consulted the council of the Greeks as to what should be done.
1.20. From it the Lacedaemonians obtained nothing more than leave to send spokesmen to the king; the Tegeans obtained pardon for their revolt, save the instigators; and the Achaeans and Eleans were ordered to give a hundred and twenty talents to the Megalopolitans, whose city had been besieged by the allies in the revolt.
1.21. Such was the end of a war which, though it arose suddenly, was nevertheless finished before Alexander overcame Darius at Arbela.
2.1. But as soon as his mind, less able to bear quiet and leisure than the affairs of war, was relieved of pressing cares, pleasures took hold of him; and the man whom the arms of the Persians had not broken, his vices conquered:
2.2. untimely banquets, and the mad sweetness of drinking deep and keeping vigil through the night, and games, and herds of concubines. Everything had slid into the foreign fashion. And by imitating that fashion as though it were better than his own, he offended the eyes and minds of his countrymen alike, so that by very many of his friends he was held as an enemy.
2.3. For he had driven men tenacious of their own discipline, and accustomed to satisfy the demands of nature with a frugal and easily procured fare, into the strange vices of conquered nations.
2.4. Hence the plots more often laid against his life, the disaffection of the soldiers, and a freer resentment amid their mutual complaints; then his own anger, now his suspicions, which an ill-considered fear stirred up, and the rest of the like, which will be told hereafter.
2.5. So, while he wore away days and nights alike in untimely banquets, he broke the surfeit of his feasts with games, not content with the throng of performers whom he had summoned from Greece; for captive women were ordered to sing, after their own fashion, a rude song jarring to foreign ears.
2.6. Among them the king often noticed one more sorrowful than the rest, and modestly reluctant as they brought her forward. She was of surpassing beauty, and her modesty set off her beauty: with her eyes cast down to the ground, and her face veiled as far as was allowed, she gave the king the impression that she was too noble to be displayed amid the games of a banquet.
2.7. So, when she was asked who she was, she answered that she was the granddaughter of Ochus, who had lately reigned in Persia, born of his son, and had been the wife of Hystaspes. He had been a kinsman of Darius, and himself a commander of a great army.
2.8. As yet some faint remnants of his former character clung to the king's mind: so, out of reverence for the fortune of one born of royal stock and for so famous a name as that of Ochus, he ordered the captive not only to be set free but to have her own possessions restored to her; her husband too was to be sought out, so that, when found, she might be given back to him as his wife.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
2.9. On the next day, moreover, he charged Hephaestion to order all the captives to be brought into the palace. There, having reviewed the rank of each, he set apart from the common throng those whose birth was eminent. There were a thousand of these; among whom was found Oxathres, the brother of Darius, more illustrious for the disposition of his spirit than for his rank.
2.10. Twenty-six thousand talents in all had been gathered from the most recent plunder: twelve thousand were spent on a largess to the soldiers, and a sum equal to this was carried off by the fraud of the guards.
2.11. Oxydates was a noble Persian, who, marked out by Darius for capital punishment, was being kept in chains: him Alexander freed and assigned the satrapy of Media, and he received the brother of Darius into the company of his friends, preserving every honor of his ancient renown.
2.12. From here they came into Parthiene, then an obscure nation, now the chief of all those which, lying beyond the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, are bounded by the Red Sea.
2.13. The Scythians had occupied the level and fertile region, troublesome neighbors even now. They have seats both in Europe and in Asia: those who dwell above the Bosphorus are reckoned to Asia, but those who are in Europe stretch in a straight tract from the left side of Thrace to the Borysthenes and thence to the Tanais.
2.14. The Tanais flows midway between Europe and Asia. Nor is it doubted that the Scythians who founded the Parthians made their way not from the Bosphorus, but from the region of Europe.
2.15. There was at that time a famous city, Hecatompylos, founded by the Greeks: there the king held a standing camp, supplies being brought in from every quarter. And so a rumor, the vice of an idle soldiery, spread abroad without an author, that the king, content with what he had achieved, had resolved to return at once into Macedonia.
2.16. They ran about, like men distracted, to their tents and made their packs ready for the march: you would have believed a signal had been given for the whole camp to gather their baggage. From here the uproar of men asking after their tent-mates, and there of men loading the wagons, was carried to the king.
2.17. The Greek soldiers, ordered home, had lent credit to the rashly spread rumor: since to each of their cavalry six thousand denarii had been given, and to each of the foot a thousand, they too believed that the end of their service was at hand.
2.18. Not otherwise than was fitting was the king terrified, who had resolved to traverse the Indies and the farthest parts of the East; and he gathered the commanders of his forces into the headquarters, and, with tears welling up, complained that he was being recalled from the very midst of his course of glory, and would carry home into his country the fortune rather of a conquered man than of a conqueror:
2.19. nor was it the cowardice of his soldiers that stood in his way, but the envy of the gods, who had set a sudden longing for their country in the hearts of the bravest men—men who a little later would return into the same lands with greater praise and renown.
2.20. Then indeed each for himself offered his service, demanded all that was most difficult, promised the obedience of the soldiers too, if he would but soothe their spirits with a gentle and fitting speech:
2.21. they had never gone away broken and cast down, as often as they had been able to drink in his eagerness and the spirit of so great a mind. He answered that he would do so; let them only prepare for him the ears of the common soldiers. And when all that seemed to bear on the matter had been sufficiently arranged, he ordered the army to be called to assembly, before which he delivered a speech of this kind:

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
3.1. "When you consider the greatness of the things we have done, soldiers, it is by no means strange that both a longing for rest and a surfeit of glory should come over you.
3.2. To say nothing of the Illyrians, the Triballians, Boeotia, Thrace, Sparta, the Achaeans, the Peloponnese—some of which I subdued under my own leadership, others under my command and auspices—
3.3. behold, having begun the war from the Hellespont, we have delivered the Ionians and Aeolis from the servitude of an unbridled barbarism; Caria, Lydia, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Paphlagonia, Pamphylia, the Pisidians, Cilicia, Syria, Phoenicia, Armenia, Persia, the Medes, Parthiene—all these we hold in our power.
3.4. I have embraced more provinces than others have captured cities, and I know not whether, in my reckoning, the very multitude of these things has not let some of them slip from me.
3.5. And so, if I believed the possession of the lands we have subdued with such speed to be secure enough, then indeed, soldiers, I would break away to my household gods, to my mother and my sisters and the rest of my fellow citizens, even though you sought to hold me back, so that there above all I might enjoy with you the praise and glory we have won, where the richest rewards of victory await us—the joy of children, of wives, of parents; peace, rest, the untroubled possession of what we have gained by valor.
3.6. But in a new and—if we will confess the truth—a precarious empire, while the barbarians still bend their stiff necks beneath its yoke, there is need of time, soldiers, while they are steeped in gentler dispositions and a better habit softens their savage natures.
3.7. The crops too await their ripening at a fixed season: so even those things, void of all sense, nevertheless mellow by their own law.
3.8. What? Do you believe that so many nations, accustomed to the rule and the name of another, bound to us by no rites, no manners, no common use of language, have been subdued by the same battle in which they were conquered? They are held by your arms, not by their own manners; and those who fear us when present will be our enemies in our absence. We are dealing with wild beasts, which, when caught and shut up, the longer time tames, because their own nature cannot.
3.9. And even now I speak as though everything that was under the sway of Darius had been subdued by arms. Nabarzanes has seized Hyrcania; not only does the parricide Bessus possess Bactra, but he even threatens us; the Sogdians, the Dahae, the Massagetae, the Sacae, the Indians are their own masters.
3.10. All these, the moment they see our backs, will follow them: for they are of the same nation, while we are foreigners and strangers.
3.11. And each man obeys his own people more peaceably, even when one rules over him who can be feared the more. Therefore either what we have taken must be given up, or what we have not must be seized. Just as in sick bodies, soldiers, physicians leave nothing that will do harm, so let us cut away whatever stands in the way of our empire. A small spark, despised, has often kindled a great fire. Nothing in an enemy is safely despised: the man you have scorned you make the stronger by your neglect.
3.12. Not even Darius received the empire of the Persians by inheritance, but was admitted to the throne of Cyrus by the favor of Bagoas, a eunuch: do not believe that Bessus will seize an empty throne with great labor.
3.13. We have indeed sinned, soldiers, if we conquered Darius for this—to hand his empire over to his slave, who dared the last crime: he held his own king, even when in need of foreign help, even one whom we as victors would have spared, like a captive in chains, and at the last, lest he could be saved by us, slew him.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
3.14. Will you suffer this man to reign? Whom I, for my part, am eager to see nailed to the cross, paying the deserved penalty to all kings and nations, and to the good faith which he violated.
3.15. But, by Hercules, if presently it shall be announced to you that this same man is laying waste the cities of the Greeks or the Hellespont, with what grief will you be filled that Bessus has seized the rewards of your victory? Then you will be in haste to recover them, then you will take up arms. But how much better to crush him while he is still terrified and scarcely master of his mind!
3.16. A four days' march remains for us, who have trampled so many snows, crossed so many rivers, run over so many mountain ridges. No sea swelling up and seizing the road with its waves delays us as we go; no defiles and narrows of Cilicia shut us in: all is level and downhill.
3.17. We stand upon the very threshold of victory. A few fugitives and the murderers of their own master remain to us. A splendid work, by Hercules, and to be counted among the foremost of your glories, you will hand down to posterity and to fame, that you avenged Darius too, your enemy, by the slaughter of the parricides, your hatred of him ended after his death, and that no impious man escaped your hands.
3.18. When this is accomplished, how much more obedient do you think the Persians will be, when they understand that you undertake righteous wars and are angry at the crime of Bessus, not at their own name?"
4.1. The speech was received with the utmost eagerness of the soldiers, bidding him lead wherever he would.
4.2. Nor did the king check their impulse; and on the third day he penetrated through Parthiene to the borders of Hyrcania, having left Craterus with the forces he commanded and the band which Amyntas led, with six hundred cavalry and as many archers added, to protect Parthiene from the incursions of the barbarians.
4.3. He ordered Erigyius to lead the baggage by the road across the plain, with a moderate escort. He himself, with the phalanx and the cavalry, having covered a hundred and fifty stades, fortified a camp in the valley by which men approach Hyrcania. A grove, shadowy with very tall and thick trees, covers the rich soil of the valley, watered by streams that flow from the overhanging rocks.
4.4. From the very roots of the mountains the river Stiboetes pours forth, which for about three stades flows all in one channel, then, beaten back by a rock that breaks its bed, opens two courses as though its waters were divided.
4.5. From there, a torrent and made more violent by the roughness of the rocks through which it runs, it plunges headlong beneath the earth. For three hundred stades it glides hidden, and then again, as if conceived from another spring, it issues forth and forms a new channel, broader than in its earlier part—
4.6. for it spreads to a breadth of thirteen stades—and again, confined by narrower banks, forces its way along. At last it falls into another river: its name is the Rhidagnus.
4.7. The inhabitants affirmed that whatever was let down into the cavern nearer to the spring came up again where the river opens its other mouth: and so Alexander ordered cattle to be cast in where the waters go beneath the earth, whose bodies, when it bursts forth again, those who had been sent to receive them saw thrown up.
4.8. Now for the fourth day he had given his soldiers rest in the same place, when he received a letter from Nabarzanes, who had intercepted Darius along with Bessus, the substance of which was this: that he had not been an enemy to Darius, but had even advised him of what he believed to be useful, and, because he had given the king faithful counsel, had nearly been killed by him.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
4.9. That Darius had been minded to entrust the guardianship of his person, against right and divine law, to a foreign soldier, condemning the loyalty of his own countrymen, which they had kept inviolate toward their kings for two hundred and thirty years.
4.10. That he himself, standing on a steep and slippery place, had taken his counsel from present necessity. Darius too, when he had killed Bagoas, had satisfied his countrymen with this excuse, that he had slain a man who plotted against him.
4.11. That nothing was dearer to wretched mortals than the breath of life: by love of it he had been driven to the last extremity.
4.12. But that he had followed those things rather than wished for them. In a common calamity each man has his own fortune. If the king should order him to come, he would come without fear. He did not fear that so great a king would violate a pledge once given: it was not the way of a god to be deceived by a god.
4.13. But if he to whom he should give his pledge seemed unworthy, many places of exile lay open to the fugitive: his country was wherever a brave man should choose a seat for himself.
4.14. Nor did Alexander hesitate to give his pledge, in the manner in which the Persians received it, that he should be unharmed if he came. Nevertheless he went in a hollow square, in order of battle, sending scouts ahead from time to time to explore the ground.
4.15. The light-armed led the column, the phalanx followed it, behind the infantry came the baggage. Both the warlike nation and the difficulty of the country's situation in the approach had heightened the king's care.
4.16. For an unbroken valley lies open all the way to the Caspian Sea, into which the arms, as it were, of that land run out: in the middle, with a slight curve, they form a bay very like the moon when the horns stand out and the star does not yet fill its whole orb.
4.17. The Cercetae and the Mossyni and the Chalybes are on the left, and on the other side the Leucosyrians and the plains of the Amazons: the former it faces where it inclines to the north, the latter where it turns to the west.
4.18. The Caspian Sea, fresher than the others, nourishes serpents of vast size: the colors of the fish in it are far different from those elsewhere. Some call it the Caspian, some the Hyrcanian; there are others who think that the Maeotian marsh falls into it, and bring as proof that its water, being fresher than the other seas, is sweetened by the inflow of the marsh's water.
4.19. From the north a vast sea presses upon the shore and drives its waves far, and over a great part lies swelling in shallows: and again, in another state of the weather, it draws the channel back into itself, and, ebbing with the same force with which it had spread, restores the land to its own nature. And some have believed that it is not the Caspian Sea, but that the Ocean falls from India into Hyrcania, whose level, as was said above, is lowered by the unbroken valley.
4.20. From here the king advanced twenty stades by a path almost impassable, overhung by woods, and torrents and floods delayed his march; yet, with no enemy in the way, he made his way through and came at last to more cultivated parts.
4.21. Besides the other provisions, of which the region then had abundance, a vast quantity of fruit also is produced, and the soil is most fertile for the growing of vines.
4.22. A common tree has the appearance of an oak, whose leaves are steeped with much honey; but unless the inhabitants gather it before sunrise, the juice is dried up even by a moderate warmth.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
4.23. Thirty stades farther he had advanced, when Phrataphernes met him, surrendering himself and those who had fled after the death of Darius; and, having received these kindly, he came to the town of Arvae. Here Craterus and Erigyius met him.
4.24. They had brought Phradates, the governor of the nation of the Tapurians; he too, received into protection, was to many an example for making trial of the king's clemency.
4.25. Then he gave the satrapy of Hyrcania to Amminaspes: this man, an exile in the reign of Ochus, had come to Philip. He restored the nation of the Tapurians too to Phradates.
5.1. And now he had entered the farthest parts of Hyrcania, when Artabazus, whom we have said above was most faithful to Darius, met him with the kinsmen of Darius and his own children and a moderate band of Greek soldiers.
5.2. The king offered his right hand to him as he came; for he had been a guest-friend of Philip, when he was an exile in the reign of Ochus, and the loyalty he had kept to his own king to the very end outweighed the pledges of that guest-friendship.
5.3. Received courteously, then, he said: "You indeed, O king, I pray the gods, may flourish in unbroken happiness: I, glad in all else, am tormented by this one thing, that in my headlong old age I cannot long enjoy your goodness." He was in his ninety-fifth year.
5.4. Nine young men, all born of the same mother, accompanied their father: these Artabazus brought to the king's right hand, praying that they might live so long as they were useful to Alexander.
5.5. The king for the most part made his journey on foot: then he ordered horses to be brought up for himself and Artabazus, lest, if he himself went on foot, the old man should be ashamed to be carried on horseback.
5.6. Then, when the camp had been pitched, he ordered the Greeks whom Artabazus had brought to be called together; but they answered that, unless pledge were given to the Lacedaemonians and the Sinopeans too, they would deliberate what they ought to do.
5.7. There were envoys of the Lacedaemonians who had been sent to Darius: when he was conquered, they had attached themselves to the Greeks serving for pay among the Persians.
5.8. The king, dismissing all pledges of compacts and of faith, ordered them to come, to have such fortune as he himself should grant them. Hesitating long, with many varying their counsels, at last they promised that they would come.
5.9. But Democrates the Athenian, who had always most opposed the power of the Macedonians, despairing of pardon, ran himself through with his sword. The rest, as they had resolved, surrendered themselves to the sway of Alexander.
5.10. There were fifteen hundred soldiers, and besides these ninety envoys sent to Darius. The soldiers were distributed as reinforcement, the rest sent home, except the Lacedaemonians, whom he ordered to be handed over into custody.
5.11. The nation of the Mardi bordered on Hyrcania, rough in their way of life and given to brigandage: this alone had neither sent envoys nor seemed likely to do his bidding. So the king, indignant that a single nation should be able to bring it about that he was not unconquered, leaving his baggage with an escort, advanced with a strong band attending him.
5.12. He had made his march by night, and at first light the enemy were in sight: it was an uproar rather than a battle. The barbarians, driven down from the hills they had occupied, fled, and the nearest villages, deserted by their inhabitants, were taken.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
5.13. The inner parts of that region could not well be approached without great hardship to the army: lofty woods and pathless crags fence in the mountain ridges, and the parts that are level the barbarians had blocked with a new kind of fortification.
5.14. Trees are planted thick on purpose; their branches, while still tender, they bend by hand, and, twisting them, set them again in the ground: from there, as if from another root, the trunks grow up more luxuriantly green.
5.15. These they do not allow to grow up where nature carries them; for they interweave one with another as in a kind of mesh. When these are clothed with much foliage, they cover the ground: and so the branches, hidden like snares, shut off the road with an unbroken hedge.
5.16. The only way was to open the pass by cutting; but this too was a work of great labor. For frequent knots had hardened the stems, and the branches of the trees, entwined with one another and like hanging hoops, baffled the strokes with their pliant withes.
5.17. The inhabitants, moreover, accustomed to creep under the thickets in the manner of wild beasts, had then too entered the pass and harried the enemy with hidden weapons. The king, searching their lurking-places like a hunter, ran many of them through, and at last ordered the soldiers to surround the pass, so that, if there were any opening, they might burst in.
5.18. But in the unknown places most of them wandered astray, and some were taken, among whom was the king's horse—they called him Bucephalas—whom Alexander valued not in the same spirit as the other beasts. For that horse would not suffer another to sit on his back, and when the king wished to mount, of his own accord lowering his knees, he would receive him; and he was believed to be conscious of whom he carried.
5.19. So, goaded by anger and grief greater than was seemly, the king ordered the horse to be tracked, and proclaimed through an interpreter that, unless they restored him, not one of them should live. Terrified by this denunciation, they brought the horse along with their other gifts.
5.20. But not even so appeased, he ordered the woods to be cut down, and earth, heaped up from the mountains, to be piled upon the plain that was blocked by the branches.
5.21. Already the work had risen to some height, when the barbarians, despairing that the region they had occupied could be held, surrendered their nation. The king, having received hostages, ordered them to obey Phradates.
5.22. Then on the fifth day he returned to his standing camp. Then he sent Artabazus home with double the honor that Darius had given him. Now they had come to the city of Hyrcania, in which had been the palace of Darius: there Nabarzanes, having received a pledge, met him, bringing vast gifts.
5.23. Among these was Bagoas, a eunuch of singular beauty and in the very flower of his boyhood, whom Darius had used and Alexander soon used: and chiefly moved by his entreaties, he pardoned Nabarzanes.
5.24. There was, as was said above, a nation of the Amazons bordering on Hyrcania, dwelling about the river Thermodon, in the plains of Themiscyra.
5.25. They had as queen Thalestris, ruling over all who dwelt between the Caucasus and the river Phasis. She, fired with a longing to see the king, departed from the borders of her kingdom, and, when she was not far off, sent men ahead to make known that the queen had come, eager to approach him and to make his acquaintance.
5.26. At once leave was granted to come, the rest being ordered to halt. Attended by three hundred women she advanced; and as soon as the king was in sight, she herself leaped down from her horse, carrying two lances in her right hand.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
5.27. The dress of the Amazons is not drawn over the whole body: for the left side is bare to the breast, the rest is then covered. Yet the fold of the garment, which they gather in a knot, does not descend below the knees.
5.28. One breast is kept untouched, with which to nourish their female children: the right is seared, so that they may bend their bows and brandish their weapons the more easily.
5.29. With undismayed countenance Thalestris gazed at the king, surveying with her eyes a bearing by no means equal to the fame of his deeds; for among all barbarians there is reverence for majesty of person, and they think none capable of great deeds but those whom nature has deigned to endow with extraordinary appearance.
5.30. But when she was asked whether she wished to seek anything, she did not hesitate to confess that she had come to share children with the king, being a woman worthy that he should beget from her heirs of his realm: the female offspring she would keep, the male she would give back to the father.
5.31. Alexander asked whether she wished to serve in war with him: but she, pleading that she had left her kingdom without a guard, persisted in her petition, that he would not suffer her to depart frustrated of her hope.
5.32. The woman's desire for love, keener than the king's, prevailed upon him to halt for a few days. Thirteen days were spent in compliance with her longing. Then she made for her kingdom, the king for Parthiene.
6.1. Here indeed he openly let loose his desires, and turned his self-restraint and moderation—those goods eminent in every loftiest fortune—into pride and wantonness.
6.2. Holding the manners of his fathers and the wholesomely tempered discipline of the Macedonian kings and their citizen-like bearing as too mean for his greatness, he strove to rival the loftiness of the Persian court, equal to the power of the gods:
6.3. he demanded that men prostrate themselves on the ground before him in worship, and that he steep so many conquerors of nations little by little in servile offices, and make them the equals of captives.
6.4. And so he set upon his head a purple diadem picked out with white, such as Darius had worn, and put on Persian dress, not even fearing the omen, that he was passing from the insignia of a victor into the garb of the conquered.
6.5. And he indeed said that he was wearing the spoils of the Persians; but with those spoils he had put on their manners too, and the arrogance of his bearing followed upon the insolence of his spirit.
6.6. The letters too which he sent into Europe he sealed with the gem of his old ring; on those he wrote into Asia the ring of Darius was impressed, so that it might appear that one mind could not contain the fortune of two.
6.7. His friends, indeed, and the cavalry, and with them the leading men of the soldiery—spurning it, yet not daring to refuse—he had adorned with Persian garments.
6.8. Three hundred and sixty-five concubines, as many as Darius had had, filled the palace, whom troops of eunuchs, themselves too accustomed to suffer a woman's part, attended.
6.9. These things, tainted with luxury and foreign manners, the old soldiers of Philip, a people raw in their taste for pleasures, openly turned away from; and throughout the whole camp there was one feeling and one talk among all, that more had been lost by victory than had been sought by war:
6.10. that at that very moment they themselves were being conquered, surrendered to alien and foreign manners. With what face, then, would they return home as though in a captive's garb? They were now ashamed of themselves; the king, made from an emperor of Macedonia into a satrap of Darius, was more like the conquered than the conquerors.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
6.11. He, not ignorant that both the leading men of his friends and the army were grievously offended, tried to recover their goodwill by liberality and gifts. But, I suppose, to free men the price of servitude is unwelcome.
6.12. Therefore, lest the matter should turn into mutiny, the leisure had to be broken by war, the material for which was opportunely at hand.
6.13. For Bessus, having taken up the royal dress, had ordered himself to be called Artaxerxes, and was drawing together the Scythians and the rest who dwell by the Tanais. This Satibarzanes reported: him, received into protection, the king set over the region he had held before.
6.14. And since the column, heavy with spoils and the apparatus of luxury, could scarcely be moved, he ordered first his own baggage, then that of the whole army, save what was strictly necessary, to be brought together into the middle.
6.15. There was a spacious plain, into which they had brought the laden wagons. While all awaited what he would then command, he ordered the beasts to be led away, and, fire being first set to his own baggage, the rest to be burned.
6.16. They were ablaze, their masters burning the very things which they had often saved from the flames to carry off untouched from the cities of the enemy, no one daring to bewail the price of his blood, when the same fire consumed the royal wealth.
6.17. Soon, however, reason soothed their grief, and, fit for service and ready for anything, they rejoiced that they had made the sacrifice of their baggage rather than of their discipline.
6.18. So they were making for the Bactrian region. But Nicanor, the son of Parmenion, carried off by a sudden death, had filled all with great longing for him.
6.19. The king, sorrowful above all, desired indeed to halt and be present at the funeral; but the scarcity of supplies compelled him to hasten: so Philotas was left with two thousand one hundred men, to pay the last rites to his brother, while he himself pressed on against Bessus.
6.20. As he was making his march, a letter was brought to him from the neighboring satraps, from which he learned that Bessus indeed was advancing against him with a hostile mind and an army, but that Satibarzanes, whom he himself had set over the satrapy of the Arii, had revolted from him.
6.21. So, although Bessus was pressing upon him, yet, judging it best to turn aside first to crush Satibarzanes, he led out the light-armed and the cavalry, and, having briskly made the march through the whole night, came upon the enemy unawares.
6.22. On learning of his arrival, Satibarzanes with two thousand cavalry—nor could more be gathered on a sudden—fled to Bactra; the rest occupied the nearest mountains.
6.23. There is a sheer crag where it faces the west, the same lowered to a gentler slope where it inclines to the east: set thick with many trees, it has a perennial spring, from which water flows in abundance.
6.24. Its circuit comprises thirty-two stades. On the summit is a grassy plain: on this they bid the unwarlike multitude settle. They themselves, where the crag rests on the ground, pile up trunks of trees and rocks.
6.25. There were thirteen thousand armed men. Leaving Craterus to besiege them, he himself hastened to pursue Satibarzanes. But, because he had learned that he was farther off, he returned to storm those who had occupied the heights of the mountains.
6.26. And at first he ordered all that men could pass over to be cleared; then, as crags and sheer rocks met them in the way, the labor seemed in vain, nature standing in the way.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
6.27. He, being ever of a spirit that struggled against difficulties, since both to advance was hard and to turn back dangerous, turned himself to all manner of thoughts, one after another—as is wont to happen when we condemn each first plan—his mind suggesting them.
6.28. As he hesitated, fortune supplied the counsel that reason could not. There was a strong west wind, and the soldier, forcing a path through the rocks, had cut down much timber. This, parched by the heat, had caught and burned with a blaze:
6.29. so he ordered other trees to be heaped up and fuel given to the fire, and quickly, the stems piled high, the height of the mountain was made level.
6.30. Then, fire cast in from every side, it caught hold of everything. The wind drove the flame into the faces of the enemy; a vast smoke, as with a kind of cloud, had hidden the sky.
6.31. The woods rang with the burning, and even those parts which the soldier had not set on fire, taking the flame, scorched all that was nearest. The barbarians tried to escape the last of torments, wherever the fire died down at all; but where the flame gave place, the enemy stood in the way.
6.32. So they were destroyed by a varied slaughter: some flung themselves into the midst of the fire, others from the rocks; some offered themselves to the hands of the enemy; a few, half-burned, came into his power.
6.33. From here he returned to Craterus, who was besieging Artacana. He, having made all ready, was awaiting the king's arrival, yielding to him, as was fitting, the title of the captured city.
6.34. So Alexander ordered the towers to be brought up; and the barbarians, terrified at the very sight, began to beg from the walls, holding out their upturned hands, that he would reserve his anger for Satibarzanes, the author of the revolt, and spare suppliants surrendering themselves. The king, granting pardon, not only raised the siege but restored all their own to the inhabitants.
6.35. As he was departing from this city, a reinforcement of new soldiers met him: Zoilus had brought five hundred cavalry from Greece, Antipater had sent three thousand from Illyricum, there were a hundred and thirty Thessalian cavalry with Philip, and from Lydia had come two thousand six hundred foreign soldiers, with three hundred cavalry of the same nation following.
6.36. With this band added, he came to the Drangae: it is a warlike nation. The satrap was Barzaentes, a partner with Bessus in the crime against his own king: he, in fear of the punishments he had deserved, fled into India.
7.1. Now for the ninth day the standing camp had been pitched, when the king, safe from external force, nay unconquered, was assailed by a crime within.
