7.2. Dymnus, a man of moderate authority and favor with the king, burned with love of a youth named Nicomachus, bound by the obedience of one body devoted to him alone.
7.3. He, as could be seen even from his face, like one stunned, with witnesses removed, withdrew with the young man into a temple, declaring beforehand that he was bringing matters secret and to be kept silent;
7.4. and, while the youth hung in expectation, he begged him, by their mutual affection and the pledges of each other's hearts, to affirm by an oath that he would cover with silence what he should confide.
7.5. And he, supposing that nothing would be disclosed which had to be revealed even at the cost of perjury, swore by the gods present.
7.6. Then Dymnus revealed that a plot had been prepared against the king for the third day, and that he himself was a partner in that design with brave and illustrious men.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
7.7. When the youth heard this, he steadfastly denied that he had pledged his faith for a parricide, and that he could be bound by no oath to conceal a crime.
7.8. Dymnus, frantic with love and fear, embracing the youth's right hand and weeping, begged at first that he would become a partner in the design and the deed:
7.9. if he could not bring himself to that, that at least he would not betray him, of whose goodwill toward himself he had, besides all else, this strongest pledge too, that he had entrusted his own life to a faith as yet untried.
7.10. At last, as he persisted in turning from the crime, he tried to terrify him with fear of death: from that head the conspirators would begin a most splendid deed.
7.11. Then, calling him now effeminate and womanishly timid, now a betrayer of his lover, now promising free gifts, and at times even a kingdom, he worked upon the spirit of the youth, who shrank far from so great a crime.
7.12. Then, setting his drawn sword now to the other's throat, now to his own, suppliant and threatening at once, he wrung from him at last that he would promise not only silence but even his help.
7.13. For Nicomachus, of a thoroughly steadfast spirit and worthy to be chaste, had changed nothing of his former resolve, but, feigning that he was caught by love of Dymnus, pretended to refuse nothing.
7.14. He then went on to inquire with whom Dymnus had entered into the partnership of so great a deed: it mattered most what kind of men were to set their hands to so memorable a work.
7.15. He, unsound with love and crime alike, both gave thanks and congratulated himself that he had not hesitated to join himself to the bravest of the young men: Demetrius, a bodyguard, Peucolaus, Nicanor: to these he added Aphobetus, Iolaus, Theoxenus, Archepolis, Amyntas.
7.16. Dismissed from this conversation, Nicomachus reported to his brother—Cebalinus was his name—what he had heard. They decided that he himself should stay in his tent, lest, if he entered the palace, being unaccustomed to approach the king, the conspirators should learn that they had been betrayed.
7.17. Cebalinus himself took his stand before the vestibule of the palace—for no nearer approach lay open to him—waiting for someone from the first cohort of the king's friends, by whom he might be brought in to the king.
7.18. By chance, the rest having been dismissed, Philotas alone, the son of Parmenion—for what cause is uncertain—had remained in the palace: to him Cebalinus, with troubled face bearing the marks of great agitation, disclosed what he had learned from his brother, and bade him report it to the king without delay.
7.19. Philotas, having praised him, at once went in to Alexander, and, much talk being spent on either side about other matters, reported nothing of what he had learned from Cebalinus.
7.20. Toward evening, as he came out, the young man met him in the vestibule of the palace, asking whether he had carried out the charge. He, pleading that the king had not been at leisure for his speech, departed.
7.21. On the next day Cebalinus was at hand as Philotas came to the palace, and reminded him, as he entered, of the matter shared with him the day before. He answered that he was attending to it:
7.22. yet not even then did he disclose to the king what he had heard. Cebalinus had begun to suspect him: so, thinking he must interrupt no further, he revealed to a noble young man—Metron was his name—set over the armory, what crime was being prepared.
7.23. He, having hidden Cebalinus in the armory, at once showed to the king, who chanced to be tending his body, what the informer had reported.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
7.24. The king, having sent guards to seize Dymnus, entered the armory. There Cebalinus, transported with joy, said: "I have you safe, snatched from the hands of the impious."
7.25. Then Alexander, having inquired into what had to be known, learned the whole in order.
7.26. And again he pressed to ask how many days it was since Nicomachus had brought him the information. And when the man confessed that it was now the third, judging that he reported what he had heard so long after with no untainted faith, he ordered him to be bound.
7.27. But he began to cry out that at the very moment he had heard it, he had hurried to Philotas; from him he was awaiting what should be discovered.
7.28. The king, asking again and again whether he had approached Philotas, whether he had pressed him that they should come to himself, and as the man persisted in affirming what he had said, stretching his hands to heaven, with tears flowing, complained that this thanks had been rendered to him by one once the dearest of his friends.
7.29. Meanwhile Dymnus, not unaware for what cause he was summoned by the king, gravely wounded himself with the sword with which he chanced to be girded, and, checked by the running up of the guards, was carried into the palace.
7.30. Looking at him, the king said: "What so great a wrong did I plan against you, Dymnus, that Philotas should seem to you worthier than I myself of the kingdom of the Macedonians?" His voice had already failed him: and so, with a groan and his face turned from the sight of the king, sinking down at once, he expired.
7.31. The king, having ordered Philotas to come into the palace, said: "Cebalinus has deserved the last punishment, if for two days he concealed a plot prepared against my life: but of this charge he sets up Philotas as the guilty party, to whom he affirms that he reported the information at once.
7.32. By how much nearer a degree of friendship you touch me, by so much the greater is the crime of your dissimulation, and I confess that this befits Cebalinus rather than Philotas. You have a favorable judge, if at least what ought not to have been admitted can be cleared away."
7.33. To this Philotas, by no means trembling, if his spirit were to be judged by his face, answered that Cebalinus had indeed reported to him the talk of a catamite, but that he himself had believed nothing on so light an authority, fearing lest he should have brought a quarrel between a lover and his minion, not without the laughter of others:
7.34. since Dymnus had killed himself, however the matter stood, it ought not to have been kept silent. And, embracing the king, he began to beg that he would look rather to his past life than to his fault, and that one of silence only, not of any deed.
7.35. I could not easily say whether the king believed him or suppressed his anger deeper: he offered his right hand as a pledge of reconciled favor, and said that the information seemed to him to have been despised rather than concealed.
8.1. Then, having summoned a council of his friends, to which, however, Philotas was not admitted, he ordered Nicomachus to be brought in.
8.2. He set forth in order the same things his brother had reported to the king.
8.3. Craterus was dear to the king among a few, and on that account opposed to Philotas through rivalry of rank; nor was he ignorant that Philotas had often been burdensome to Alexander's ears by his excessive boasting of his valor and his service, and that for these things he was suspect, not indeed of crime, but of insolence.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
8.4. Judging that no other occasion fitter for crushing his rival would arise, he set the appearance of loyalty before his hatred: "Would," he said, "that at the very beginning of this matter too you had deliberated with us!
8.5. We would have advised, if you wished to pardon Philotas, that you should rather suffer him to remain ignorant how much he owed you, than, brought to the fear of death, more often to think of his own peril than of yours through your kindness. For he will always be able to plot against you, you will not always be able to pardon Philotas.
8.6. Nor is there cause for you to think that one who has dared so much can be changed by pardon. He knows that those who have used up mercy can hope for no more.
8.7. But I, even if he himself, overcome either by repentance or by your kindness, should wish to be quiet, know that his father Parmenion, the leader of so great an army and placed not far below the height of your greatness by his long-established authority among his own soldiers, will not owe you with an even mind the safety of his son.
8.8. Some kindnesses we hate. It is shameful to confess that one has deserved death: it remains that he prefer to seem to have suffered a wrong rather than his life. Therefore know that you must fight with them for your safety.
8.9. Enough enemies remain, to pursue whom we are about to go: fortify your flank against domestic enemies. If you remove these, I fear nothing from the foreigner." Thus Craterus.
8.10. Nor did the rest doubt that he would not have suppressed the information of the conspiracy unless he were the author or a partner. For what man, dutiful and of a good mind—not a friend only, but one of the lowest commons—on hearing what had been reported to him, would not have run at once to the king?
8.11. The son of Parmenion, the commander of the cavalry, the arbiter of all the king's secrets, had not been moved even by the example of Cebalinus, who reported to him at once what he had learned from his brother! He had even pretended that the king was not at leisure for his speech, lest the informer should seek another go-between.
8.12. Nicomachus, bound also by the religion of the gods, had hastened to unburden his conscience: Philotas, having spent almost the whole day in sport and jest, had grudged to insert a few words touching the king's life into so long and perhaps superfluous a conversation.
8.13. But he had not believed the boys who brought such reports! Why, then, had he dragged out two days, as though he gave credit to the information? Cebalinus ought to have been dismissed, if he condemned his report.
8.14. In his own peril each man has a great spirit: when there is fear for the king's safety, men ought to be credulous, to admit even those who report idle tales.
8.15. All therefore decreed that an inquiry should be held concerning him, that he might be forced to disclose the partners in the crime. The king, having warned them to keep the design in silence, dismissed them. He then ordered the march for the next day to be proclaimed,
8.16. lest any mark of the design entered upon should be given to the guilty. Philotas was even invited to the king's last banquet, and the king brought himself not only to dine with, but even to converse familiarly with, the man he had condemned.
8.17. Then, at the second watch, the lights being put out, Hephaestion and Craterus and Coenus and Erigyius came to the palace with a few men—these of the friends—and of the bodyguards, Perdiccas and Leonnatus. Through these it was commanded that those who kept watch at the headquarters should keep vigil under arms.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
8.18. Already cavalry had been posted at all the approaches, ordered too to beset the roads, lest anyone should escape secretly to Parmenion, who was then in command of Media and of great forces.
8.19. Atarrhias, moreover, had entered the palace with three hundred armed men: to him ten attendants were added, each of whom was followed by ten armed men.
8.20. These were distributed to seize the other conspirators; Atarrhias, sent with three hundred against Philotas, set himself to force the closed entrance of the house, attended by fifty of the readiest young men: for he had ordered the rest to surround the house on every side, lest Philotas should be able to slip away by a hidden exit.
8.21. He, whether through tranquillity of mind or through weariness, sleep had overcome, relaxed: Atarrhias seized him while still torpid.
8.22. At last, his slumber being shaken off, as the chains were thrown upon him, he said: "The bitterness of my enemies, O king, has conquered your goodness." And, having spoken no more, with his head veiled, they led him into the palace.
8.23. On the next day the king proclaimed that all should assemble under arms. About six thousand soldiers had come, and besides them a throng of sutlers and camp-servants had filled the palace.
8.24. The armor-bearers screened Philotas with their column, lest he should be seen by the common soldiers before the king had addressed them.
8.25. In capital matters the king made inquiry after the ancient custom of the Macedonians, the army judged—in peace it was the right of the common people—and the power of the kings availed nothing, unless their authority had first availed.
8.26. So first the corpse of Dymnus was brought in, most being ignorant of what he had prepared or by what chance he had been killed.
9.1. Then the king came forward into the assembly, bearing on his face the grief of his soul. The sadness of his friends too had raised no small expectation of the matter.
9.2. For a long time the king stood with his face cast down to the ground, like one stunned and dazed; at last, recovering his spirit, he said: "I was almost, soldiers, snatched from you by the crime of men: by the providence and mercy of the gods I live. And the sight of you, which I revere, has compelled me to be the more vehemently angry at the parricides, since this is the first—nay, the only—fruit of my life, that I am still able to render thanks to so many bravest men who have deserved most excellently of me."
9.3. The groaning of the soldiers interrupted his speech, and tears welled up in all. Then the king said: "How much greater a stir shall I raise in your minds, when I show the authors of so great a crime! Their mention I still shrink from, and, as though they could be saved, I abstain from their names.
9.4. But the memory of our former affection must be overcome, and the conspiracy of impious citizens disclosed. But how shall I be silent on so great a wickedness? Parmenio, at his age, bound to me by so many of my services and of my father's, the oldest of all our friends, has shown himself the leader of so great a crime.
9.5. His agent Philotas suborned Peucolaus and Demetrius and now Dymnus, whose body you behold, and the rest of the same madness, against my life.
9.6. The murmur of men indignant and complaining sounded through the whole assembly on every side, such as is wont to be that of a multitude, and most of all of soldiers, when they are moved either by zeal or by anger.
9.7. Then Nicomachus and Metron and Cebalinus were brought forward, and each set forth what he had reported. By none of their information was Philotas marked out as a partner in the crime. So the cry of indignation was met in turn by silence.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
9.8. Then the king said: "Of what spirit, then, does he seem to you, who suppressed the information of this matter when it was reported to him? That it was not idle, the end of Dymnus declares.
9.9. Bringing an uncertain matter, Cebalinus did not fear the rack, nor did Metron put off even a moment of time to unburden himself, so that he burst in where I was bathing: Philotas alone feared nothing, believed nothing.
9.10. O man of great spirit! Would that man be moved by the king's peril, change his countenance, hear with anxiety the informer of so great a matter?
9.11. There lies hidden, without doubt, a crime beneath that silence, and a greedy hope of the kingdom has driven a headlong spirit to the last wickedness. His father commands Media: he himself, mighty among the many leaders of forces through my strength, breathes greater things than he can grasp.
9.12. My childlessness too, that I am without children, is despised. But Philotas errs. In you I have children, parents, kinsmen: while you are safe I cannot be childless.
9.13. Then he read out an intercepted letter of Parmenion, which he had written to his sons Nicanor and Philotas, by no means presenting the information of any graver design.
9.14. For its substance was this: 'First take care of yourselves, then of your own: for thus shall we accomplish what we have determined.'
9.15. And the king added that it was so written that, whether it reached the sons or not, it could be understood by those in the secret, or, if intercepted, deceive the ignorant.
9.16. But Dymnus, when he named the rest of the partners in the crime, did not name Philotas! This indeed is a sign not of his innocence but of his power, that he is so feared even by those by whom he can be betrayed, that, when they confess about themselves, they nevertheless conceal him. For the rest, his own life informs against Philotas.
9.17. This man joined himself as ally and accomplice to Amyntas, who was my cousin and who in Macedonia prepared impious plots against my life. This man gave his sister in marriage to Attalus, than whom I had no graver enemy.
9.18. This man, when I had written to him, by the right of so familiar an intimacy and friendship, what answer had been given by the oracle of Jupiter Hammon, brought himself to write back that he indeed congratulated me on being received into the number of the gods, but pitied those who must live under one who exceeded the measure of a man.
9.19. These are the signs of a spirit long since estranged from me and envious of my glory. These indeed, soldiers, as long as I could, I pressed down in my own heart. For I seemed to myself to be tearing away a part of my own vitals, if I made cheaper to myself those on whom I had bestowed such great things.
9.20. But now it is not words that must be punished: the rashness of the tongue has come to the sword.
9.21. These, if you believe me, Philotas whetted against me; if you believe himself, he admitted them. Whither shall I betake myself, soldiers? To whom shall I entrust my life? Over the cavalry, the best part of the army, over the leaders of the noblest youth, I set him; my safety, my hope, my victory I committed to his faith and protection.
9.22. His father I advanced to the same height in which you yourselves placed me; Media, than which no region is richer, and so many thousands of citizens and allies I subjected to his command and sway. Whence I had sought protection, peril arose.
9.23. How happily I should have fallen in battle, the prey of an enemy rather than the victim of a citizen! Now, saved from the perils which alone I feared, I have fallen into these, which I ought not to have feared.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
9.24. You are wont, soldiers, ever and again to ask of me that I spare my own safety. You yourselves can grant me what you urge me to do. To your hands, to your arms I flee: against your will I do not wish to be safe; with your will I cannot be, unless I am avenged."
9.25. Then he ordered Philotas to be led in, his hands bound behind his back, veiled in a worn-out cloak. It was easily apparent that men were moved at so pitiable a state, not without ill will toward one a little before beheld with admiration.
9.26. The day before they had seen him commander of the cavalry, they knew he had taken part in the king's banquet: suddenly they beheld him not a defendant only, but already condemned, nay bound.
9.27. There came too into their minds the fortune of Parmenion also, so great a leader, so renowned a citizen, who, lately bereaved of two sons, Hector and Nicanor, was now, with the one whom calamity had left him, pleading his cause in his absence.
9.28. So Amyntas, a royal commander, stirred up again with a harsh speech against Philotas the assembly that was inclining to pity: that they had been betrayed to the barbarians; that no one would return to his wife in his country and to his parents; that, like a trunk of a body with its head removed, without breath, without a name, they would be the mockery of the enemy in a foreign land.
9.29. By no means as he himself hoped was Amyntas's speech welcome to the king, because he had reminded them of their wives, of their country, as pledges to make them perform their other duties.
9.30. Then Coenus, although he had united Philotas's sister to himself in marriage, nevertheless inveighed against Philotas more keenly than anyone, crying out that he was a parricide of the king, of his country, of the army, and snatched up a stone
9.31. that chanced to lie before his feet, meaning to hurl it at him, as most believed, wishing to snatch him from the torture. But the king stayed his hand, affirming that the accused ought first to be given the power of pleading his cause, and that he would not suffer it to be judged otherwise.
9.32. Then, ordered to speak, Philotas, whether from consciousness of crime or from the greatness of his peril, frantic and stunned, dared neither to lift his eyes nor to open his mouth.
9.33. Then, as the tears flowed and his spirit failed, he sank upon the man who held him, and, his eyes wiped with that man's cloak, gradually recovering breath and voice, he seemed about to speak.
9.34. And now the king, looking at him, said: "The Macedonians are about to judge you: I ask whether you will use your native tongue with them."
9.35. Then Philotas said: "Besides the Macedonians, there are present very many whom I think will more easily grasp what I shall say, if I use the same language which you have used, for no other reason, I suppose, than that your speech might be understood by the greater number."
9.36. Then the king said: "Do you see how Philotas loathes even his native tongue? He alone, indeed, scorns to learn it. But let him speak, by all means, however it pleases him, only remember that he shrinks from our manners as much as from our speech."
10.1. And so the king departed from the assembly. Then Philotas said: "It is easy for an innocent man to find words; it is hard for a wretched one to keep a measure in words.
10.2. And so, left destitute between the best conscience and the most unjust fortune, I know not how to obey both my own mind and the time.
10.3. The best judge of my cause is indeed absent: why he himself has been unwilling to hear me, I cannot, by Hercules, conceive, since to him, the cause being known on both sides, it is as lawful to condemn me as to acquit, but, the cause unknown, I cannot be freed in his absence, who have been condemned by him when present.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
10.4. But although the defense of a man in chains is not only superfluous but even hateful—since he seems not to instruct the judge, but to arraign him—yet, however far I am allowed to speak, I will not desert myself, nor allow myself to seem condemned even by my own verdict.
10.5. For my part, of what crime I am accused I do not see: among the conspirators no one names me, of me Nicomachus said nothing, Cebalinus could not know more than he had heard.
10.6. And yet the king believes that I was the head of the conspiracy! Could Dymnus, then, pass over the man he followed, especially when, as he sought allies, I should have been named even falsely, that the man who was being tempted might be the more easily driven on?
10.7. For it was not after the crime was detected that he passed over my name, so that he might seem to have spared an accomplice: to Nicomachus, whom he believed would keep his secret silent, he confessed, and, others being named, he alone withdrew me.
10.8. I ask you, fellow soldiers, if Cebalinus had not approached me, had wished me to know nothing of the conspirators, should I today be pleading my cause, when no one names me?
10.9. Grant that Dymnus still lives and wishes to spare me—what of the rest? Those who will confess about themselves will, forsooth, withdraw me! Calamity is malignant, and the guilty man, for the most part, when he is tortured by his own punishment, finds rest in another's.
10.10. Will so many accomplices, not even set upon the rack, confess the truth? And yet no one spares a man about to die, nor does a dying man, I think, spare anyone.
10.11. To the true charge, and the one charge, I must return: why did you keep silent the matter reported to you? why did you hear it so unconcerned? This, whatever it is, since I have confessed it, you, Alexander, wherever you are, have forgiven me: I embraced your right hand, the pledge of a reconciled spirit, I took part in your banquet too.
10.12. If you believed me, I am acquitted; if you spared me, I am dismissed: at least keep to your own judgment. What did I do this last night, after I left your table? what new crime, reported to you, changed your mind?
10.13. I was resting in a heavy sleep, when my enemies, by binding me as I slept among my woes, woke me. Whence comes so deep a quiet of sleep to a parricide and a traitor?
10.14. The wicked, with conscience clamoring against them, cannot fall asleep: the Furies harry them when the parricide is but conceived, much more when it is accomplished. But to me my innocence first, then your right hand, had given security: I did not fear that another's cruelty should have more power with you than your own clemency.
10.15. But that you may not repent of having believed me—the matter was reported to me by a boy who could produce neither witness nor pledge of his information, one likely to fill all with fear, if he had begun to be heard.
10.16. I believed, unhappy man, that my ears were being thrust into the quarrel of a lover and his minion, and held his report suspect, because he did not report it himself, but rather suborned his brother.
10.17. I feared lest he should deny that he had charged Cebalinus with it, and I should seem to have been the cause of peril to many of the king's friends.
10.18. Even so, though I have harmed no one, I have found men who would rather I perished than be safe: what enmities do you think I should have incurred, if I had assailed the innocent?
10.19. But Dymnus killed himself! Could I, then, divine that he would do so? By no means. So that which alone gave credit to the information could not move me when I was interrupted by Cebalinus.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
10.20. But, by Hercules, if I had been privy with Dymnus to so great a crime, I ought not, in those two days, to have concealed that we were betrayed: Cebalinus himself could have been removed, and with no trouble.
10.21. Finally, after the information was reported, which I was about to cover, I alone entered the king's bedchamber, girt indeed with iron. Why did I put off the deed? Was it that without Dymnus I did not dare?
10.22. He, then, was the head of the conspiracy! under his shadow I, Philotas, lay hid—I, who aim at the kingdom of the Macedonians! Has any one of you been corrupted with gifts? What leader, what commander did I court too earnestly?
10.23. Against me it is indeed objected that I spurn the fellowship of the native tongue, that I disdain the manners of the Macedonians. So I, forsooth, threaten an empire which I scorn! Long since that native speech has fallen out of use through intercourse with other nations: a foreign tongue must be learned by victors as well as by the vanquished.
10.24. These things, by Hercules, do not wound me more than that Amyntas, the son of Perdiccas, plotted against the king. That I had friendship with him I do not refuse to defend, if the king's brother ought not to have been loved by us.
10.25. But if one set in that rank of fortune had even to be revered, am I, I ask, guilty because I did not divine the future, or must the innocent friends of the impious die too? If that is just, why have I lived so long? if unjust, why am I now nevertheless slain?
10.26. But I wrote that I pitied those who must live under one who believed himself the son of Jupiter. Faith of friendship, perilous freedom of true counsel, you have deceived me! you drove me not to keep silent what I felt!
10.27. I confess that I wrote these things to the king, not about the king. For I was not making him an object of ill will, but fearing for him. Alexander seemed to me worthier to acknowledge the stock of Jupiter in silence than to boast of it by proclamation.
10.28. But since the credit of the oracle is sure, let the god be the witness of my cause: keep me in chains while Hammon is consulted, whether I have entered upon a secret and hidden crime. He who deigned to name our king his son will not suffer any of those who plotted against his own stock to lie hidden.
10.29. If you believe tortures to be surer than oracles, I do not even beg off from this means of exhibiting the truth.
10.30. Men accused of capital crimes are wont to bring their parents before you. Two brothers I lately lost; my father I can neither show nor dare to invoke, since he himself too is accused of so great a crime.
10.31. For it is too little that he, but now the parent of so many children, resting content in his one son, should be bereaved of him too, unless he himself be set upon my pyre.
10.32. So, dearest father, both for my sake will you die, and with me: I take your life, I extinguish your old age. Why did you beget me, unhappy man, the gods opposing? was it that you might reap from me these fruits which await you?
10.33. I know not whether my youth be more wretched or your old age: I am snatched away in the very strength of my years; from you the executioner will take that breath which, had fortune been willing to wait, nature was demanding.
10.34. The mention of my father has reminded me how timidly and hesitatingly I ought to have disclosed what Cebalinus had reported to me. For Parmenion, when he had heard that poison was being prepared for the king by the physician Philip, wished to dissuade him, by a letter written, from drinking the medicine which the physician had resolved to give. Was credit given to my father? did his letter have any authority?

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
10.35. How often have I myself reported what I had heard, and been repulsed with mockery of my credulity! If we are both hated when we inform and suspected when we are silent, what ought we to do?"
10.36. And when one out of the throng of bystanders had cried out: "Not to plot against your benefactors!"
10.37. Philotas said: "Rightly, whoever you are, you speak. And so, if I plotted, I do not beg off the penalty, and I make an end of speaking, since my last words have seemed grievous to your ears." Then he was led away by those who guarded him.
11.1. There was among the leaders one Bolon, vigorous of hand, raw in the arts of peace and in civil bearing, an old soldier, promoted from a humble rank to the place in which he then was:
11.2. who, while the rest were silent, fierce with a stolid boldness, began to remind them how often each man, thrust out of the lodgings he had taken, had had to give them up to the scum among Philotas's slaves, from the very place whence he had driven his comrades.
11.3. That his vehicles, laden with gold and silver, had stood through whole villages, and that not one of his comrades had been received even into the neighborhood of his lodging, but, by men set to guard his sleep, all had been banished far off, lest that woman of his be roused by the murmuring of men, truer in silence than in sound.
11.4. That they had been his mockery, called rustics and Phrygians and Paphlagonians—he who, born a Macedonian, did not blush to hear men of his own language through an interpreter.
11.5. That now he wished Hammon to be consulted: but that the same man had accused Jupiter of falsehood for acknowledging Alexander as his son, fearing, forsooth, lest what the gods offered should breed ill will.
11.6. That when he plotted against the life of the king and his friend, he had not consulted Jupiter: now he sent to the oracle, while his father stirred up those over whom he commanded in Media, and with money, the keeping of which had been committed to him, drove abandoned men to the partnership of the crime.
11.7. That they themselves would send to the oracle, not to ask of Jupiter what they had learned from the king, but to give thanks, to pay their vows for the safety of the best of kings.
11.8. Then indeed the whole assembly was kindled, and a beginning was made by the bodyguards, crying out that the parricide must be torn to pieces by their hands. This indeed Philotas, who feared graver punishments, heard with no very unwilling spirit:
11.9. but the king, having returned into the assembly, whether to torture him in custody too, or to learn the whole more carefully, put off the council to the next day; and, although the day was drawing toward evening, nevertheless ordered his friends to be summoned.
11.10. And to the rest indeed it seemed good that he should be overwhelmed with stones after the manner of the Macedonians; but Hephaestion and Craterus and Coenus said that the truth must be wrung out by tortures: and even those who had advised otherwise went over to the opinion of these.
11.11. The council, then, being dismissed, Hephaestion with Craterus and Coenus rose to hold the inquiry concerning Philotas.
11.12. The king, having summoned Craterus and held a conversation with him, the substance of which was not made public, withdrew into the innermost part of his lodging, and, the witnesses removed, awaited the outcome of the inquiry far into the night.
11.13. The torturers set out before the eyes of Philotas all the instruments of cruelty.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
11.14. And he of his own accord: "Why do you delay," he said, "to kill the king's enemy, the murderer who confesses? What need is there of inquiry? I planned it, I willed it." Craterus pressed that what he confessed he should say under torture too.
11.15. Then he is seized, and, while his eyes were bandaged, while his garment was stripped off, he invoked in vain, on deaf ears, the gods of his fathers and the laws of nations. Then, through the utmost torments—since he was both condemned and tortured by enemies to win the king's favor—he was mangled.
11.16. And at first, although on this side fire, on that the lash were now applied not for inquiry but for punishment, he kept in his power not only his voice but even his groans:
11.17. but after his body, swelling with sores, could not bear the strokes of the scourges driven against his bare bones, he promised that, if they would set a measure to the tortures, he would tell what they sought to know.
11.18. But he wished them to swear by the safety of Alexander that there would be an end of the inquiry, and that the torturers should be removed.
11.19. And when both were obtained: "Craterus," he said, "tell me what you wish me to say." When the other indignantly said that he was mocking him, and again recalled the torturers, he began to ask for time, until he should recover his breath, meaning to disclose all that he knew.
11.20. Meanwhile the cavalry, all the noblest and chiefly those who were joined to Parmenion by near kinship, after report had spread abroad that Philotas was being tortured, fearing the law of the Macedonians, by which it was provided that the kinsmen of those who had plotted against the king should be put to death together with them, some killed themselves, others fled into pathless mountains and vast solitudes, a vast terror being spread through the whole camp, until the king, on learning of the disturbance, proclaimed that he remitted the law concerning the punishment of the kindred of the guilty.
11.21. Whether Philotas wished to free himself from torture by truth or by falsehood is a doubtful conjecture, since the same end of pain is set both for those who confess the truth and for those who tell lies.
11.22. But: "You are not ignorant," he said, "how familiarly my father lived with Hegelochus: that Hegelochus, I mean, who fell in battle: he was to us the cause of all our ills.
11.23. For when the king first ordered himself to be saluted as the son of Jupiter, he, taking it ill, said: 'Do we then acknowledge as king this man who disdains Philip as his father? It is all over with us, if we can endure such things.
11.24. He despises not only men but even the gods, who demands to be believed a god. We have lost Alexander, we have lost our king: we have fallen upon a pride tolerable neither to the gods, with whom he makes himself equal, nor to men, from whom he sets himself apart.
11.25. Have we made a god of our own blood, to despise us? to be burdened with coming into the assembly of mortals? Believe me, we too, if we are men, shall be adopted by the gods.
11.26. Who avenged the death of this man's great-grandfather Alexander, who then of Archelaus, who of Perdiccas, slain?
11.27. This man indeed pardoned his father's murderers.' These things Hegelochus said over supper: and on the next day at first light I am summoned by my father. He was sad, and saw me sorrowful: for we had heard things that bred anxiety.
11.28. So, that we might test whether he had poured out those words weighed down with wine, or had conceived them from a deeper design, it pleased us to summon him. He came, and, the same talk being repeated of his own accord, he added that, if we dared to be leaders, he would claim for himself the next part after us; if courage failed us, he would cover the design with silence.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
11.29. To Parmenion, while Darius still lived, the thing seemed untimely: for they would be killing Alexander not for themselves but for the enemy; but with Darius removed, the reward of the king slain—Asia and the whole East—would fall to his murderers. And the design being approved, on these terms faith was both given and received.
11.30. As to what concerns Dymnus, I know nothing, and, having confessed these things, I understand that it does not avail me that I am free of the present crime."
11.31. They, the tortures being applied again, when with the very spear-shafts they beat his face and eyes, wrung from him that he should confess this charge too.
11.32. Then, as they demanded that he should set forth the order of the contemplated crime, since they seemed likely to detain the king long at Bactra, he answered that he had feared lest his father, seventy years old, the leader of so great an army, the keeper of so much money, should in the meantime be cut off, and there should be for himself, stripped of so great forces, no cause for killing the king.
11.33. That he had therefore hastened, while the reward was in his hands, to put the design into effect: and that, unless they believed his father absent from it, he did not, although he could no longer bear them, refuse the tortures.
11.34. They, having conferred, judging that enough had been inquired, returned to the king, who on the next day ordered both what Philotas had confessed to be read out, and the man himself, because he could not walk, to be carried in.
11.35. While he acknowledged everything, Demetrius, who was accused of being a partner in the most recent crime, was brought forward. With much affirmation and equal steadfastness of spirit and of face denying that anything had been contemplated by him against the king, he even demanded the tortures upon himself:
11.36. when Philotas, casting his eyes about, as they fell upon a certain Calas standing not far off, ordered him to come nearer. As the man, troubled, refused to pass over to him, he said: "Will you suffer Demetrius to lie and me to be tortured again?"
11.37. Calas's voice and blood had failed him, and the Macedonians suspected that Philotas wished to defile the innocent, because the young man had been named neither by Nicomachus nor by Philotas himself when he was tortured: but when he saw the king's officers standing around him, he confessed that he and Demetrius had contemplated that crime.
11.38. So all who had been named by Nicomachus were, the signal being given after the custom of their fathers, overwhelmed with stones.
11.39. From great peril not of his life only but also of ill will Alexander had been freed: for Parmenion and Philotas, the leading men of his friends, could not have been condemned, unless plainly guilty, without the indignation of the whole army.
11.40. And so, while the inquiry was doubtful, while he denied the crime, he seemed to be cruelly tortured: after his confession even the pity of his friends was idle.
1.1. The soldiers had judged that Philotas, his guilt still fresh in its traces, was justly delivered to execution; yet once the man they had hated was no more, their resentment turned to pity.
1.2. They were moved also by the young man's renown, and by the old age and bereavement of his father.
1.3. Parmenion had been the first to open Asia to the king; the sharer of all his dangers, he had always held one wing in the line of battle; he had been Philip's friend before all others, and so loyal to Alexander himself that when there was need to kill Attalus the king would use no other agent than him.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
1.4. The recollection of these things passed through the army, and seditious murmurs were carried back to the king. He, in truth not greatly disturbed and prudent enough, judging that the faults of leisure are dispelled by occupation, issued an edict that all should present themselves in the forecourt of the royal quarters.
1.5. When he saw them gathered in great numbers, he came forward to an assembly. Without doubt by prior arrangement, Atarrhias began to demand that Alexander the Lyncestian, who long before Philotas had wished to kill the king, should be brought forth.
1.6. Denounced by two informers, as we have said above, he had now been kept in chains for a third year. It was established beyond doubt that this same man had conspired with Pausanias in the murder of Philip as well; but because he had been the first to hail Alexander as king, he had been spared the penalty rather than the charge.
1.7. At that time too the entreaties of Antipater, his father-in-law, delayed the king's just anger. But now the festering grief broke out afresh: for the care of present peril revived the memory of the old danger.
1.8. So Alexander was led out from confinement and ordered to speak; and although he had rehearsed his defence for three whole years, yet, hesitating and trembling, he brought out only a few of the words he had composed, and at last not his memory only but his very mind failed him.
1.9. No one doubted that his trembling was the sign of a guilty conscience and not a failure of memory. And so those who were standing nearest, while he still struggled against his forgetfulness, ran him through with their lances.
1.10. When his body had been carried away, the king ordered Amyntas and Simmias to be brought in; for Polemon, the youngest of the brothers, on learning that Philotas was being tortured, had fled.
1.11. These had been the dearest of all the friends of Philotas, advanced to great and honourable charges chiefly by his support; and the king remembered that they had been won over to himself by Philotas with the utmost zeal, nor did he doubt that they too had shared in this last design.
1.12. So he complained that they had long been suspect to him because of his mother's letters, in which he had been warned to guard his life against these men; but that, reluctantly believing the worse, he had now, overcome by manifest proofs, ordered them put in chains.
1.13. For on the day before the crime of Philotas was uncovered, it could not be doubted that they had been with him in secret. And their brother, who had fled when the inquiry into Philotas was being made, had himself disclosed by his flight the cause of it.
1.14. Lately, contrary to their custom, on the pretext of duty, when the rest had been removed to a distance, they had attached themselves to his side with no plausible reason; and he, wondering why they were not performing such service in their turn, and alarmed by their very agitation, had withdrawn briskly to the armour-bearers who were following close behind.
1.15. To this was added the fact that, when Antiphanes, the secretary of the cavalry, had ordered Amyntas, on the day before the crime of Philotas was detected, to give from his own horses, as the custom was, to those who had lost theirs, Amyntas had answered arrogantly that, unless Antiphanes desisted from his purpose, he would soon learn who he himself was.
1.16. Now the violence of his tongue and the rashness of the words which they had hurled against the king himself were nothing else than the mark and witness of a guilty mind. If these things were true, they had deserved the same fate as Philotas; if false, he himself required them to refute them.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
1.17. Antiphanes was then brought forward and gave evidence about the horses not handed over and the arrogant threats added besides.
1.18. Then Amyntas, leave to speak being granted, said: "If it matters nothing to the king, I ask that, while I speak, I may be freed from my chains." The king ordered both to be loosed; and when Amyntas asked that the dress of an armour-bearer also be restored to him, he ordered a lance to be given him.
1.19. When he had grasped it in his left hand, avoiding the spot where the body of Alexander the Lyncestian had a little before lain, he said: "Whatever end awaits us, O king, we confess that we shall owe a happy one to you, and lay a sadder one to the account of fortune.
1.20. We plead our case without prejudice, our bodies and minds free; you have even restored the dress in which we are accustomed to attend you. Our case we are able to plead; our fortune we shall cease to fear.
1.21. And I beg you to permit me to defend first that which was charged against me last. We, O king, are not conscious to ourselves of any speech uttered against your majesty. I would say that you long ago overcame envy, were there not danger that you might believe other things, said more spitefully, to be excused by a flattering oration.
1.22. But even if some harsher word of your soldier — whether failing and weary on the march, or in peril in the line of battle, or sick in his tent and tending his wounds — has reached your ears, we had earned, by our brave deeds, that you should prefer to charge such words to our circumstances rather than to our minds.
1.23. When anything grievous befalls us, we are all guilty: we raise hostile hands against our own bodies, which surely we do not hate; if parents or children meet us, they are both ungrateful and hateful in our sight. On the other hand, when we are honoured with gifts, when we return laden with rewards, who can endure us?
1.24. Who can restrain that eagerness of spirit? Neither the indignation nor the joy of soldiers is moderate: we are swept by impulse into every passion. We blame and praise, we pity and grow angry, just as the present emotion has moved us: now we long to march to India and the Ocean, now the memory of wives and children and country meets us.
1.25. But these thoughts, these voices of men talking together, the signal given by the trumpet ends: each of us runs to his own ranks, and whatever wrath has been conceived in the tent is poured out upon the heads of the enemy.
1.26. Would that Philotas too had sinned within the bounds of words! And so I will return to that for which we are accused. So far am I from denying the friendship which we had with Philotas, that I confess we even sought it, and reaped great profit from it.
1.27. Or do you wonder that the son of Parmenion, whom you wished to be next to yourself, surpassing in dignity almost all your friends, was courted by us?
1.28. You yourself, by Hercules, if you wish to hear the truth, O king, are the cause of this peril to us. For who else brought it about that those who wished to please you ran to Philotas? Handed on by him, we rose to this degree of your friendship: he it was, in your presence, whose favour we might seek and whose anger we might fear.
1.29. If we did not swear almost in your very words, yet we all, you leading the way, swore that we would hold the same men for enemies and friends as you held. Bound by this oath of loyalty, were we then to turn away from the man whom you set above all?
1.30. Therefore, if this is a crime, you have few innocent men — nay, by Hercules, none. For all wished to be the friends of Philotas, but only as many as wished it could not be so. And so, if you do not separate friends from accomplices, neither will you separate from his friends those who only wished to be the same.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
1.31. What sign of a guilty conscience, then, is brought forward? As I suppose, because on the day before he spoke with us familiarly and without witnesses. But I could not clear myself, had I on that day changed anything from my old life and manner. Now, indeed, if on that day too, which is held suspect, we did as on all other days, custom will wash away the charge.
1.32. But we did not give horses to Antiphanes, and that on the day before Philotas was exposed. Here my business is with Antiphanes. If he wishes to make us suspect because we did not give him horses on that day, he himself, because he demanded them, will not be able to clear himself.
1.33. For the charge hangs in doubt between the man who keeps and the man who demands, except that the case of him who does not surrender his own is better than that of him who asks for another's.
1.34. Moreover, O king, I had ten horses; of these Antiphanes had already distributed eight to those who had lost their own, and I myself had but two; and when that most arrogant man — most unjust, certainly — wished to take these away as well, I was forced to keep them, unless I were willing to serve on foot.
1.35. Nor do I deny that I spoke with the spirit of a free man to that most cowardly fellow, who usurped this one right of warfare, that he might distribute other men's horses to those about to fight. For to such a pass of misfortune has it come, that I must excuse my words at once to Alexander and to Antiphanes!
1.36. But, by Hercules, my mother wrote to you about us as your enemies. Would that she had been more prudently anxious for her son, and had not, with a troubled mind, conjured up empty phantoms as well! Why does she not add the cause of her fear? Why does she not at last point out her authority? By what deed or word of ours was she moved to write you so alarming a letter?
1.37. O wretched is my condition, since perhaps it is no less dangerous to keep silent than to speak! But however the matter is to turn out, I would rather that my defence displease you than my cause. And you will recognize what I am about to say: for you remember that, when you were sending me to bring soldiers from Macedonia, you said that many sound young men were being hidden in the house of your mother.
1.38. You charged me, therefore, to look to no one but you, and to bring to you those who shirked military service. This indeed I did, and I carried out your command more freely than was expedient for me.
1.39. Gorgias and Hecataeus and Gorgidas, whose good service you make use of, I brought from there. What, then, is more unjust than that I, who, if I had not obeyed you, was justly bound to suffer punishment, should now perish because I obeyed? For your mother has no other cause for persecuting us than that we set your advantage before a woman's favour.
1.40. Six thousand Macedonian foot and six hundred horse I brought; and part of these would not have followed me, had I been willing to indulge those who shirked service. It follows, then, that, since she is angry with us on this account, you should pacify your mother, you who exposed us to her anger."
2.1. While Amyntas was thus pleading, those who had pursued his brother Polemon, of whom we spoke before, as he fled, came up by chance, bringing him back in chains. The hostile assembly could scarcely be restrained from at once hurling stones at him, after their manner.
2.2. But he, quite undismayed, said: "I plead nothing for myself, only that my flight be not charged against the innocence of my brothers. If this cannot be defended, let it be my crime. Their case is the better for this very reason, that I, because I fled, am held suspect."

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
2.3. When he had spoken thus, the whole assembly assented; then tears began to flow from all, their feelings so suddenly turned to the opposite, that the very thing which had most offended now told in his favour.
2.4. He was a youth in the first bloom of age, just coming to manhood, whom a panic not his own had carried off amid the cavalry thrown into confusion by the torture of Philotas. Deserted by his companions and hesitating between the plan of returning and that of flight, he had been seized by those who had pursued him.
2.5. Then he began to weep and to beat his face, grieving not for his own lot, but for his brothers, who were in peril because of him.
2.6. And by now he had moved the king too, not the assembly only; but one man alone was implacable — his brother, who, gazing on him with a terrible countenance, cried out: "Then, madman, you should have wept, when you were setting spurs to your horse — deserter of your brothers and companion of deserters!
2.7. Wretch, whither and from what were you fleeing? You have brought it about that I, a man on trial for his life, must use the words of an accuser." Polemon confessed that he had sinned more grievously against his brothers than against himself. Then indeed they restrained neither their tears nor the shouts by which a multitude declares its sympathies. With one voice, uttered by common consent, they begged him to spare innocent and brave men. The friends too, an opening for mercy being given, rose and, weeping, entreated the king.
2.8. He, when silence was made, said: "I too, by my own sentence, acquit Amyntas and his brothers. But as for you, young men, I would rather you forgot my kindness than remembered your peril. Return to favour with me in the same good faith with which I myself return to you.
2.9. Had I not sifted what was laid against you, you might have suspected something of dissimulation in me: it is better to be cleared than to be suspected. Reflect that no one can be acquitted unless he has pleaded his cause.
2.10. You, Amyntas, forgive your brother. This will be, even to me, a simple pledge of your reconciled mind."
2.11. Then, the assembly dismissed, he ordered Polydamas to be summoned. He was by far the most esteemed of Parmenion's men, and accustomed to stand next at his side in the line of battle.
2.12. And although he had come into the royal quarters trusting in his innocence, yet, when he was ordered to produce his brothers, who were very young and unknown to the king on account of their age, his confidence turned into anxiety and he began to tremble, weighing more often the things that might harm him than those by which he might escape.
2.13. Already the armour-bearers to whom it had been commanded had brought them forward, when the king ordered Polydamas, bloodless with fear, to come nearer; and, when all had been removed, he said: "By the crime of Parmenion we have all alike been assailed, but most of all you and I, whom he deceived under the show of friendship.
2.14. To pursue and punish him — see how greatly I trust your loyalty — I have determined to use you as my agent. Your brothers shall be hostages while you carry this out.
2.15. Set out for Media, and carry to my prefects letters written in my own hand. There is need of speed, that you may outstrip the swiftness of rumour. I wish you to arrive there by night, and on the next day to execute what shall be written.
2.16. To Parmenion too you shall carry letters, one from me, the other written in the name of Philotas. The seal of his ring is in my power. If the father believes it stamped by his son, when he sees you, he will fear nothing."

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
2.17. Polydamas, freed from so great a fear, promised his service even more earnestly than was required; and, commended and loaded with promises, he laid aside the garment he wore and put on Arabian dress.
2.18. Two Arabs, whose wives and children meanwhile were hostages with the king as a bond of good faith, were given him as companions. Through regions desert by reason of drought they came on camels, on the eleventh day, to the place he had appointed.
2.19. And before his own arrival was announced, Polydamas again took up the Macedonian dress and at the fourth watch came to the tent of Cleander — who was a royal commander there.
2.20. Then, having delivered the letters, they arranged to come to Parmenion at first light. And already he had brought the king's letters to the others too, and already they were about to come to him, when they announced to Parmenion that Polydamas had arrived.
2.21. While he was rejoicing at the arrival of his friend, and at the same time eager to learn what the king was doing — for after a long interval he had received no letter from him — he ordered Polydamas to be sought out.
2.22. The lodgings of that region have great recesses, made pleasant with groves planted by hand: these were especially the delight of kings and satraps.
2.23. Parmenion was walking in the grove, in the midst of the commanders who had been ordered by the king's letters to kill him. They had appointed as the time for doing the deed the moment when Parmenion should begin to read the letters delivered by Polydamas.
2.24. When Polydamas, coming from afar, was seen by Parmenion with a look that presented the appearance of joy, Parmenion ran to embrace him; and, the mutual greeting made, Polydamas handed him the letter written by the king.
2.25. Parmenion, breaking the seal of the letter, asked what the king was doing. The other answered that he would learn from the letter itself.
2.26. When Parmenion had read it, he said: "The king is preparing an expedition against the Arachosians. A tireless man, and never resting! But it is time, now that so great glory has been won, that he spare himself for his own safety."
2.27. Then he began to read with joy — as could be marked from his face — the other letter written in the name of Philotas; whereupon Cleander pierced his side with his sword, then struck his throat, and the rest ran him through even when he was already lifeless.
2.28. And the armour-bearers who had stood at the first approach to the grove, when the slaughter became known, the cause of which was unknown, came into the camp and roused the soldiers with the tumultuous report.
2.29. They, in arms, gathered at the grove in which the murder had been done, and threatened, unless Polydamas and the rest who shared the same guilt were given up, to overthrow the wall set round the grove and to make atonement to their leader with the blood of all.
2.30. Cleander ordered the chief men among them to be admitted, and read out to the soldiers the king's letters, in which were contained the plots of Parmenion against the king and his prayers that they should avenge him.
2.31. So, when the king's wish was known, not indeed their indignation, but yet the sedition, was suppressed. The greater number slipping away, a few remained who begged that at least they might be allowed to bury the body themselves.
2.32. This was long refused through Cleander's fear lest he offend the king. Then, as they begged more insistently, judging that the cause of consternation must be removed, he allowed the headless trunk to be buried; the head was sent to the king.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
2.33. Such was the end of Parmenion, a man renowned in war and in peace. Many things he had done with success without the king; the king without him had done nothing of great moment. He satisfied a most fortunate king who measured all things by the standard of his own fortune. At seventy years of age he discharged the duties of a young commander, and often even those of a common soldier: keen in counsel, vigorous in action, dear to the chief men, more acceptable to the common soldiers.
2.34. Whether these qualities urged him to a desire for the throne, or only made him suspect, may be doubted; for whether Philotas, overcome by his last tortures, spoke truth — things that could not be proved by deeds — or whether he sought an end of his torments by falsehoods, was doubted even while the matter was fresh, when it might more easily have been made clear.
2.35. Alexander, judging that those whom he had learned to have freely lamented the death of Parmenion must be separated from the rest of the army, set them apart into a single cohort, and gave them as commander Leonidas, who had himself once been joined to Parmenion by intimate friendship.
2.36. They were nearly the same men whom the king had otherwise held in disfavour. For when he wished to test the temper of his soldiers, he advised that whoever had written letters to his people in Macedonia should hand them, with confidence, to those whom he himself was sending, who would faithfully deliver them. Each had written frankly to his own kin what he felt: to some the service was a burden, to most it was not unwelcome.
2.37. Thus the letters both of those who gave thanks and of those who complained were intercepted. And those who happened to have complained in their letters of weariness of toil he ordered to encamp apart from the rest in this cohort, for the sake of ignominy — meaning to use their bravery in war, and to remove their freedom of tongue from credulous ears. This counsel, rash perhaps — for the bravest of the young men were stung by the affront — the king's good fortune, like all else, turned to good.
2.38. Nothing was readier for war than they: their valour was spurred both by the desire to wipe out the disgrace and by the fact that brave deeds could not lie hidden in so small a number.
3.1. These matters thus settled, Alexander, having appointed Arsames satrap of the Drangae, ordered the march to be proclaimed against the Arimaspi, whom they were already then calling, with a changed name, the Euergetae, ever since they had aided with shelter and supplies the army of Cyrus, afflicted by cold and want of food.
3.2. It was the fifth day since he had come into that region. He learned that Satibarzanes, who had revolted to Bessus, had again broken into the country of the Arii with a band of horsemen. So he sent against him Caranus and Erigyius with Artabazus and Andronicus: six thousand Greek foot and six hundred horse followed them.
3.3. He himself in sixty days set in order the nation of the Euergetae, presenting them with a great sum of money for their notable loyalty to Cyrus.
3.4. Then, leaving Amedines — he had been a secretary of Darius — to govern them, he subdued the Arachosians, whose region reaches to the Pontic sea. There the army which had been under Parmenion met him. There were six thousand Macedonians, two hundred nobles, and five thousand Greeks with six hundred horse — without doubt the strength of all the king's forces.
3.5. Menon was given to the Arachosians as commander, four thousand foot and six hundred horse being left as a garrison. The king himself entered, with his army, the territory of a nation not well known even to its neighbours, since they cultivated no mutual intercourse by trade.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
3.6. They are called the Parapanisadae, a rustic race of men, the most uncivilized among the barbarians.
3.7. The harshness of their land had hardened the natures of the men as well. They look in great part toward the icy axis of the north; they are joined on the west to the Bactrians; their southern region slopes down to the Indian sea.
3.8. They build their huts of unbaked brick, and, because the land is barren of timber even on the bare ridge of the mountain, they use the same brickwork right up to the topmost peak of their buildings.
3.9. But the structure, broader at the bottom, is gradually, as the work rises, drawn into a narrower compass, and at last comes together in the manner most like the keel of a ship.
3.10. There, an opening being left at the top, they admit light. Vines and trees, if any have been able to endure in so great a rigour of the soil, they bury deep: in winter, dug under, they lie hidden; when, the snow scattered, the ground begins to open, they are restored to the sky and the sun.
3.11. But so deep do the snows press upon the earth, bound by frost and almost perpetual rigour, that not even the track of a bird or any wild beast appears. A dim shade of the sky, rather than light, like to night, presses on the land, so that scarcely can the things that are near be seen.
3.12. In this solitude, then, stripped of all human cultivation, the army endured whatever of hardship can be borne: want, cold, weariness, despair.
3.13. The unaccustomed and excessive rigour killed many; it burned the feet of many, the eyes of most. Above all it was deadly to the exhausted: for in the very frost their failing bodies sank down, and when these had ceased to move, the force of the cold so bound them fast that they could not strain to rise again.
3.14. The numbed men were roused by their comrades, and there was no other remedy than to force them to walk: then at last, the vital heat being stirred, some vigour returned to their limbs.
3.15. Those who were able to reach the huts of the barbarians were quickly restored. But so thick was the gloom that nothing but smoke showed where the buildings were.
3.16. The natives, who had never before seen a stranger in their lands, when they suddenly caught sight of armed men, were paralysed with fear and brought out whatever was in their huts, begging that their own persons be spared.
3.17. The king went round the column on foot, raising some of the fallen and supporting others, when they could hardly keep up, with the help of his own body. Now at the foremost standards, now in the middle, now in the rearmost part of the column, he was present, multiplying his own toil along the march.
3.18. At last they came to more cultivated regions, and the army was revived by an abundant supply of provisions; and at the same time those who had not been able to keep up came into that camp.
3.19. From there the column advanced to Mount Caucasus, whose ridge divides Asia with an unbroken chain: on this side it looks toward the sea that washes Cilicia, on that toward the Caspian gulf and the river Araxes and the famous deserts of the Scythian region.
3.20. Taurus, a mountain of the second magnitude, joins itself to Caucasus: rising from Cappadocia, it passes by Cilicia and is linked to the mountains of Armenia.
3.21. Thus the ridges, cohering among themselves as if in a continuous series, have an unbroken back, from which almost all the rivers of Asia descend, some into the Red, some into the Caspian, some into the Hyrcanian and the Pontic sea.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
3.22. In a space of seventeen days the army crossed the Caucasus. A rock upon it embraces ten stades in circuit and rises four in height; on this, antiquity has handed down, Prometheus was bound.
3.23. A site was chosen for founding a city at the foot of the mountain. To seven thousand of the subdued nations, and besides to those soldiers whose service the king had ceased to use, it was permitted to settle in the new city. This too the inhabitants called Alexandria.
4.1. But Bessus, terrified by the speed of Alexander, having duly performed sacrifice to the gods of his country, as is the custom with those nations, was taking counsel of the war with his friends and the commanders of his forces amid the feasting.
4.2. Heavy with wine, they began to extol their own strength and to despise now the rashness, now the small numbers, of the enemy.
4.3. Bessus above all, fierce in words and arrogant with the kingdom won by crime, and scarcely master of his mind, began to say that the fame of the enemy had grown through the sloth of Darius.
4.4. For he had met them in the narrowest passes of Cilicia, when by falling back he might have drawn his unwary foes into places safe by their natural situation — so many rivers thrown in their way, so many fastnesses of the mountains, among which the enemy, once caught, would have had no chance of flight, let alone of resistance.
4.5. His own plan was to withdraw into the country of the Sogdiani: he would set the river Oxus like a wall against the enemy, while strong reinforcements gathered from the neighbouring peoples.
4.6. There would come, he said, the Chorasmii and the Dahae and the Sacae and the Indians and the Scythians who dwell beyond the river Tanais: of whom none was so lowly that his shoulders could not reach the head of a Macedonian soldier.
4.7. The drunken men cried out together that this was the one wholesome opinion: and Bessus ordered the wine to be passed round more liberally, meaning to finish off Alexander over the table.
4.8. There was at that banquet Gobares, a Mede by nation, but famed for the magic art — if indeed it is an art, and not the mockery of every empty fellow — more by profession than by knowledge, but otherwise temperate and upright.
4.9. When he had begun by saying that he knew it more useful for a servant to obey an order than to offer counsel, since the same fate awaits those who obey as awaits the rest, but those who advise incur a peril of their own, Bessus bade him speak without fear, and even handed him the cup that he held in his hand.
4.10. Taking it, Gobares said: "The nature of mortals can be called perverse and ill-disposed on this account also, that each man is duller in his own affairs than in another's.
4.11. The counsels of those who advise themselves are troubled. Fear stands in the way, sometimes desire, sometimes a natural love of the things you have devised: for arrogance does not befall you. You have at any rate found by experience that you deem whatever you yourself discover either the only or the best course.
4.12. You bear a great burden upon your head, the royal emblem: this must either be borne with moderation, or — which I abhor — it will fall upon you.
4.13. There is need of counsel, not of impulse." Then he added what was commonly used among the Bactrians, that a timid dog barks more fiercely than it bites, and that the deepest rivers glide with the least sound. These things I have inserted, that whatever prudence could exist among barbarians might be recorded.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
4.14. By these words he had held his hearers in suspense. Then he disclosed counsel more useful to Bessus than welcome. "In the forecourt of your palace," he said, "stands a most swift king: he will move his army before you move that table.
4.15. Now you would summon an army from the Tanais and set rivers against arms. As though, by the way you mean to flee, the enemy cannot follow! The road is common to both, and safer for the victor. Though you may think fear a swift thing, yet hope is swifter.
4.16. Why do you not rather seize the favour of the stronger and surrender yourself, since, however it falls out, you, by surrendering, will have a better fortune than as an enemy?
4.17. You hold a kingdom not your own, that you may the more easily lose it. You might perhaps begin to be a just king, when he himself, who can both give you a kingdom and snatch it away, has made you so.
4.18. You have faithful counsel, which it is needless to pursue at greater length. A noble horse is governed even by the shadow of the whip; a sluggish one cannot be roused even by the spur."
4.19. Bessus, fierce both by nature and from much wine, blazed up so far that he could scarcely be restrained by his friends from killing him — for he had even drawn his scimitar. Certainly he sprang up from the banquet, in no way master of his mind. Gobares, slipping away amid the tumult, deserted to Alexander.
4.20. Bessus had eight thousand Bactrians under arms. These, as long as they had believed that the Macedonians, on account of the inclemency of the sky, would make for India rather, had obediently done his bidding: but after it was learned that Alexander was approaching, they slipped away, each to his own village, and left Bessus.
4.21. He, with a band of dependants who had not changed their allegiance, having crossed the river Oxus and burned the boats by which he had crossed, lest the enemy use the same, was gathering new forces among the Sogdiani.
4.22. Alexander had indeed crossed the Caucasus, as has been said above; but for want of grain it had come almost to the point of famine.
4.23. They anointed their limbs with oil pressed from sesame, just as with olive oil; but of this oil each jar was valued at two hundred and forty denarii, honey at three hundred and ninety, wine at three hundred: of wheat there was nothing, or very little, to be found.
4.24. Siri the barbarians called the pits which they conceal so cleverly that none but those who dug them can find them: in these the corn lay stored.
4.25. For want of these the soldiers were sustained on river fish and herbs. And now these very foods had failed, when they were ordered to slay the pack-animals on which they carried their burdens: on the flesh of these, until they reached the Bactrians, they prolonged their lives.
4.26. The nature of the Bactrian land is manifold and varied. In one part many a tree and vine nourishes abundant and mild fruits; rich soil is watered by frequent springs; the gentler parts are sown with grain, the rest yield pasture for herds.
4.27. Then a great part of the same land is held by barren sands: parched with squalid drought, the region nourishes neither man nor crop. But when winds blow from the Pontic sea, they sweep together whatever sand lies on the plains; and when this is heaped up, it has from afar the appearance of great hills, and all the traces of the former path are lost.
4.28. And so those who cross the plains watch the stars by night, like sailors, and by their course direct their way: and the shade of night is almost brighter than the daylight.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
4.29. Therefore by day the region is trackless, because they find no track to follow, and the brightness of the stars is hidden by the gloom. Moreover, if that wind which rises from the sea catches any, it buries them in the sand.
4.30. But where the land is gentler, a great multitude of men and horses is bred. And so the Bactrians had made up thirty thousand horse.
4.31. Bactra itself, the capital of that region, is situated beneath Mount Parapanisus. The river Bactrus passes by its walls. This gave its name to the city and the region.
4.32. While the king was keeping his quarters there, the revolt of the Peloponnesians and the Spartans was announced from Greece — for they had not yet been defeated when those set out who were to announce the beginnings of that uprising — and another present terror was brought, that the Scythians who dwell beyond the river Tanais were coming to bring aid to Bessus. At the same time, what Caranus and Erigyius had done among the nation of the Arii was reported. A battle had been joined between the Macedonians and the Arii.
4.33. The deserter Satibarzanes commanded the barbarians; and when he saw the fight standing sluggish on both sides, with equal forces, he rode up to the foremost ranks, and, his helmet removed, when those who were hurling weapons had been checked, he challenged to combat any who wished to fight man to man: he would have his head bare in the contest.
4.34. Erigyius could not endure the ferocity of the barbarian commander — a man heavy in years, indeed, but to be ranked behind none of the young men in strength of mind and body. He, his helmet removed and showing his grey hairs, said: "The day has come on which I shall show, either by victory or by a most honourable death, what manner of friends and soldiers Alexander has."
4.35. And, saying no more, he drove his horse against the enemy. You would have thought it commanded that both lines should hold back their weapons: they certainly withdrew at once, leaving a free space, intent on the issue not of the commanders only, but also of their own fortune — for they would follow the outcome of another's peril.
4.36. The barbarian first hurled his spear; Erigyius avoided it by a slight inclination of his head, and himself, spurring on his horse, fixed his levelled pike so deep in the middle of the barbarian's throat that it stood out through the back of his neck.
4.37. Thrown headlong from his horse, the barbarian still fought on. But Erigyius, drawing the spear from the wound, drove it again into his face. Satibarzanes, clasping it with his hand, aided the enemy's blow, that he might perish the sooner.
4.38. And the barbarians, their leader lost — whom they had followed more from necessity than of their own will — then, not unmindful of the favours of Alexander, handed over their arms to Erigyius.
4.39. The king, glad indeed at this, and in no way easy concerning the Spartans, yet bore their revolt with great spirit, saying that they had not dared to lay bare their designs until they learned that he himself had reached the borders of India.
4.40. He himself moved his forces in pursuit of Bessus; and Erigyius met him, bearing before him the head of the barbarian, the rich spoil of war.
5.1. So, the region of the Bactrians being handed over to Artabazus, he left the baggage and the impedimenta there with a garrison; and he himself, with a light column, entered the desert places of the Sogdiani, leading the army by a night march.
5.2. The want of water, as has been said before, kindled thirst by despair sooner than by the desire of drinking. Through four hundred stades not even a little moisture appears.

title: Histories of Alexander the Great
text:
5.3. The heat of the summer sun sets the sands aflame; and when these begin to burn, everything is scorched as if by a continuous conflagration.
5.4. Then a mist, stirred up by the excessive heat of the earth, hides the light, and the appearance of the plains is no other than that of a vast and deep sea.
5.5. The night march seemed bearable, because the bodies were relieved by the dew and the morning cool. But when, with the very light, the heat rises, drought absorbs all natural moisture: mouths and inner parts are burned deep within.
5.6. And so first their spirits, then their bodies, began to fail: it irked them both to halt and to advance.
5.7. A few, warned by those acquainted with the region, had prepared water: this for a little while checked their thirst, then, as the heat increased, the longing for moisture was kindled again. So whatever there was of wine and oil was poured into them; and so sweet was the drinking that they had no fear of thirst to come.
5.8. Then, heavy with the moisture greedily swallowed, they could neither carry their arms nor advance; and those whose water had failed seemed more fortunate, since these very men were forced to bring up by vomiting the liquid they had poured in without measure.
